ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
5
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Land
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.
Background
Australia was settled by Indigenous Australian people 
40,000–60,000 years ago. They established effective 
processes of hunting and gathering that rarely 
left them without food. Europeans are descended 
from people in the Fertile Crescent in Iran and Iraq, 
approximately 10,000 years ago. They focused on 
agricultural practices, which meant they alternated 
between famine and plenty.
The British often saw Indigenous Australian people as 
barbaric and ignorant, believing their own society was 
a superior civilisation. Their racist attitudes made it easy 
to decide that land without familiar rows of houses, 
cities and farms was ‘empty’. They declared Australia 
terra nullius (empty land) and felt fully justified in 
invading and colonising Australia. The racist attitudes 
of the British also led them to assume that Indigenous 
Australian people were one homogenous group. In 
reality there were at least 250–300 groups who spoke 
numerous languages (300–700 distinct languages). This 
misunderstanding led to significant social problems 
that persist today. 
The first British people who came to Australia did so 
under duress, as soldier guards and unwilling convicts, 
transported to create a penal colony. Moving to 
Australia was so unthinkable that many convicts did 
whatever they could to get out of it. However, Australia 
quickly moved from being a penal colony for criminals 
to a place of opportunity for settlers who were willing 
to work hard. Many settlers moved to Australia to grow 
crops or raise sheep and cattle. They wanted to make 
a land for themselves; something they couldn’t do in 
their home country. 
Starter activity
With the class, brainstorm ideas about what Australia 
was like in the year 1788. This is an opportunity to test 
pre-knowledge of the topic. Ask questions such as:
• 
 Who were the first British people to come to 
Australia? Why did they come here?
• 
 What was life like for Indigenous Australian people 
before European settlement in 1788?
• 
 How did Indigenous Australian people use the 
land?
• 
How did British settlers use the land?
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Map of Australia’, asks students to 
use maps as a focus for considering Australia from the 
perspectives of two groups: Indigenous Australian 
people and the first British settlers. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous Australians and their 
land’, extends the previous task by considering how 
Indigenous Australian peoples managed the land and 
comparing this to the traditional British use of land.
The Activity sheet, ‘Timeline of Australia’, identifies 
some key events from 1788 to 1918. Students are asked 
to show these events on a timeline, and then research 
three more key events from this time.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Homes in New South Wales’, 
students annotate primary source images to compare 
the temporary homes of Indigenous Australian people 
with the more permanent homes in the towns of British 
settlers.  
The Activity sheet, ‘Penal colony or pastoral settlement’, 
looks at the changing use of land by the British in 
Australia. 
Extension ideas
• 
 Have students explore the interactive map of 
Aboriginal languages at:  
http://www.abc.net.au/indigenous/map/
• 
 Students could use the above website to choose 
one language or group to research. Ask them to 
find out about the place this group lived, how they 
lived and their cultural practices and beliefs. 
Objectives
• Learn about the Australian landscape
• Consider how European colonists and 
Indigenous Australian peoples interacted with 
the land
• Identify key events that shaped the 
development of Australia
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
17
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes –The goldfields
Prior knowledge
Students need a basic understanding of the settlement 
of Australia.
Background
The gold rush in Australia started in 1851, only 
three years after the Californian gold rush in 1848. 
The mid-1800s was a period of great movement as 
people migrated first to America and later to Australia 
in the hope of finding gold. This had a large impact 
on Australia, especially in Victoria as the two main 
goldfields in the 1850s were Bendigo and Ballarat. 
These population changes contributed to the: 
• 
 construction of the Australian national identity as a 
‘working man’s paradise’ where poor men and their 
families could live a reasonable life
• 
 expansion of the city of Melbourne into ‘Marvellous 
Melbourne’, allowing it to compete with European 
cities for size and grandeur
• 
 development of racialised policies in the newly 
federated Australia – the Immigration Restriction Act.
Living on the goldfields was difficult. Miners often 
struggled to buy food and mining gear, the possibility 
of finding gold was limited and the fee for the mining 
licence at 30 shillings a month (£18 a year) to rent an 
area approximately 3.6 metres square was exorbitant. 
Facilities were initially limited in the gold mining 
region, with sanitation and housing only slowly 
following the boom. Some miners brought their 
families. So while the goldfields were full of men, there 
were also women and children. 
Due to the difficulties of life on the goldfields, many 
became disillusioned and changed occupations. 
The demand for labour in Australia meant that many 
people were paid well and could afford items that were 
seen as luxuries for the lower classes in other countries, 
such as meat for every night’s meal.
The goldfields also proved to be a useful landscape 
for developing political thought. The Eureka Rebellion 
was held on the goldfields of Ballarat as miners sought 
political representation in the government. 
The goldfields were also a place of disturbing acts 
of racism, particularly against Chinese miners. There 
were riots and attacks at a number of goldfields. In 
the Lambing Flat riots in New South Wales, many 
of the 200 Chinese miners were savagely beaten. 
Xenophobic actions and attitudes led to restrictions in 
Chinese immigration in the different colonies. These 
attitudes were later expressed in federal law with the 
Immigration Restriction Act of 1901. 
Starter activity
Many students will have prior knowledge of the gold 
rush from primary school studies. Work with the class 
to create a mind map of what they already know 
about the Australian gold rush. This can help you to 
identify the extent of their knowledge and correct any 
misconceptions about the time period.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Immigration in the gold rushes’, asks 
students to answer questions about a timeline and a 
graph. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Life on the goldfields’, students 
examine a primary source image to find out about how 
people lived and worked in the goldfields.
The Activity sheet, ‘Eureka Rebellion’, introduces key 
information about this event, and students complete 
comprehension tasks. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Women of Eureka’, provides primary 
sources that students respond to by writing a first 
person account of life during Eureka.
The Activity sheet, ‘Marvellous Melbourne’, explores 
how the city developed with a focus on sanitation.
Extension ideas
Have students create a poster for the Eureka Rebellion. 
They should use powerful images, symbols and clever 
colour choices to show the ideas and events of the 
Eureka Rebellion. Ask students to annotate their work 
to explain the reasons for their design choices.
Objectives
• Learn about the experiences of the people on 
the goldfields
• Consider the impact of the Eureka Rebellion on 
the Australian nation
• Discover how the gold rush led to the 
development of ‘Marvellous Melbourne’.

ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
23
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Non-European immigration
Prior knowledge
Students need a basic understanding of the settlement 
of Australia.
Background
The establishment of Australia as a country is 
usually strongly linked to British and European 
immigration. However, the image of early Australia as 
primarily a place of white migrants is in many ways a 
misunderstanding. Although immigration was largely 
made up of Europeans, the impact and contributions 
of immigrants from many non-European backgrounds 
should not be forgotten.
People from many different nations saw Australia as a 
land of possibility. It was a place where they could get 
jobs, find husbands or wives, try life in a new land and 
perhaps find gold. Some people from non-European 
backgrounds, such as the Kanakas from the Pacific 
Islands, were lied to, tricked and/or kidnapped to get 
them to Australia to work on the sugar cane fields. 
Others, such as the ‘Afghan’ cameleers, came willingly 
to work with the camels that suited this wild and dry 
land. Both groups were often treated with racism by 
European immigrants. The Chinese immigrants mainly 
came for the gold rush and were also mistreated and 
persecuted for being of a different race. 
In 1901 when Australia became one Federated country, 
the new government introduced the Immigration 
Restriction Act. This reduced non-European immigration 
by using techniques such as dictation tests in order 
to limit who could come to Australia. This created 
the white Australia of the 1900s which only began 
diminishing after the 1940s, before being dismantled in 
the 1970s.
Starter activity
Work with the class to brainstorm a list of countries 
from which people emigrated to Australia in the 1800s. 
If students do not mention Afghanistan, China and the 
Pacific Islands, suggest them yourself. Ask questions 
such as: Why would people move to a faraway country 
where they do not speak the language or know the 
culture?
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Chinese immigration’, discusses 
the reasons why Chinese immigrants first moved 
to Australia, how they were treated and what 
contributions they made to Australian society. 
On the Resource sheet, ‘Mongolian Octopus’, a 
primary source image is used to explore the negative 
stereotypes of Chinese people in the 1880s. 
Using the Activity sheet, ‘Racism in Australia’, students 
plan and write a short source analysis of the image on 
the Resource sheet, ‘Mongolian Octopus’.
The Activity sheet, ‘Afghans in Australia’, asks student to 
fill in the missing words to complete information about 
the contributions of the Afghan cameleers. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Blackbirding’, explores the practice 
of bringing Pacific Islanders to Australia to work as 
indentured labour on the Queensland sugar cane 
plantations.
Extension ideas
Have students research someone from their family tree. 
They could find out:
• 
why this person came to Australia
• 
 what made them want to leave their former 
country 
• 
what made them choose Australia. 
Then ask students to compare these experiences to 
those of the early Chinese, Afghan or Pacific Islander 
migrants. 
Objectives
• Learn about the immigration of non-Europeans
• Consider the racist treatment of different 
groups and the beliefs and values this 
treatment reflected
• Discover contributions of non-European 
immigrants to the formation of Australia

ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
29
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Life in 1900
Prior knowledge
A basic knowledge of Federation may be useful.
Background
By the 1900s, Australia had started to define itself 
as a nation. It had moved quickly from an isolated 
wilderness where convicts were transported to 
a relatively modern civilisation by the 1900s. The 
discovery of gold in places like Ballarat, Bendigo and 
Castlemaine led to a huge influx of migrants from a 
wide range of countries. This began to shape Australia 
into the multicultural nation it is today. 
People began viewing Australia as being at the 
forefront of egalitarianism and equality. However, in 
many ways this perception was simply a veneer that 
hid the reality: people in Australia were not equal. 
There was a vast gulf between the rich and the poor, 
sexism was rife, and those in the country had a much 
more basic existence than those in the cities.
Australian society in 1900 was on the verge of massive 
change. New technology led to improvements in 
housing, sanitation and working conditions. The 
separate colonies were to become one country with 
Federation in 1901. Women fought to be heard, 
forming suffragette groups to argue for the female vote 
to be part of Federation. Education gradually moved 
from the province of the wealthy and middle class to 
being available to all: free, secular and compulsory. 
Starter activity
Ask students to guess what life was like for people 
in Australia in 1900. Compile a class list, focusing on 
areas such as housing, transport, work, education and 
recreation. As they progress through the unit, update 
the list to reflect what they learn. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Sanitation and health’, guides 
students through a comparison of the experiences 
of the poor and the rich. It also identifies sanitation 
developments in the 1900s. 
With the Activity sheet, ‘Homes’, students compare and 
contrast their own homes with those of the working 
class living in worker’s cottages. This activity could 
be extended in class by using masking tape to mark 
out the floor plan of the worker’s cottage. This would 
provide students with a stronger understanding of the 
similarities and differences in housing today. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Working class men, women and 
children’, explores the difficulties in the lives of the 
working class. Students use this information with 
the Activity sheet, ‘Plan a story’, to plan a story set in 
Australia in the 1900s. The Activity sheet, ‘Tall tales’, 
provides information about creative writing and 
guides students through the process of writing the 
introduction to their creative short story.
Extension ideas
Have students use http://trove.nla.gov.au to research 
Australian newspapers from around 1900. You can alter 
the dates in the advanced search option or by choosing 
the decade option on the side once you have started to 
search. (Search using ‘Available online’ and ‘Australian 
content’ to find relevant information). 
Ask students to complete one of the following activities.
• 
 Find an advertisement in a newspaper from around 
1900. What items are being sold? Why were these 
items important or desirable? What persuasive 
techniques are used to advertise them?
• 
 Choose an issue that is important today, such 
as drugs, women’s rights, immigration, sports or 
gambling. Find out how this issue was presented 
around 1900. Is the way people viewed the issue 
at that time similar or different to how we see the 
issue today? Explain your answer.
• 
 Choose a nationality or race to research. How 
were people from that group described in 1900? 
Is positive or negative language used?
Objectives
• Learn about key features of life in Australia in 
the 1900s
• Consider this key moment in time as Australia 
moved from separate colonies to become a 
Federation
• Compose a fictional piece that shows an 
understanding of this historical period
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
35
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Federation
Prior knowledge
Some understanding of the settlement of Australia may 
be useful.
Background
When Australia was first settled by the British, it was 
divided into two colonies: New South Wales and New 
Holland. The British controlled New South Wales, which 
also included the modern states of Queensland and 
Victoria. New Holland was controlled by the Dutch. 
This area included Western Australia and most of 
South Australia and Northern Territory. Over time, 
the two colonies separated into Tasmania (originally 
Van Diemen’s land), Victoria, South Australia (which 
controlled Northern Territory 1863-1910), Western 
Australia, New South Wales (which controlled Northern 
Territory until 1863) and Queensland. Britain controlled 
them all.
The colonies operated as if they were separate 
countries. Each government could decide on laws 
without considering the other colonies. One advantage 
of this was that each government was free to consider 
the unique needs of the settlers in their region. One 
disadvantage was that the laws and practices of one 
colony could be significantly different to those of all 
the others. This was a problem particularly in border 
towns. Large taxes had to be paid for moving produce 
from one colony to another, even if that was to a town 
just across the border.
Starter activity
Have the class complete a dictation test to show the 
students how difficult it was to emigrate to Australia 
after 1901. These tests are real ones used in the 1930s, 
but they could be given in any European language. 
Test 1: The tiger is sleeker, and so lithe and graceful 
that he does show to the same appalling advantage as 
his cousin, the lion, with the roar that shakes the earth. 
Both are cats, cousins of our amiable purring friend of 
the hearthrug, but the tiger is king of the family.
Test 2: Ice and snow cover the Poles, which are not 
further from the sun than we are, but the sun’s rays 
reach them slantwise, and are stopped by such a 
thickness of air that not enough of them reaches the 
surface of the earth at the Poles to keep them warm.
Point out to students that the purpose of dictation tests 
was to restrict non-European immigration.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Colony to country’, outlines 
reasons why people wanted to form a federated 
country. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Reasons for Federation’, students 
match reasons from the Resource sheet, ‘Colony to 
country’, to given themes and compare them with the 
situation today. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Suffragettes’, gives students key 
information about suffragettes. They will use this 
information to complete sentences on the Activity 
sheet, ‘Suffering for suffrage’. The answers are: 
1 vote, 2 abolish, 3 novel, 4 campaign, 5 Indigenous 
Australians, 6 petitions, 7 women, Indigenous 
Australians, 8 Indigenous Australians, Referendum. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Healthy nation’, provides 
information about sickness and health, and asks 
students to come up with solutions to protect people 
from common diseases.
Extension ideas
Ask students to make a chart to explore the two 
following questions.
Why would it be better if our states and territories 
were like countries? 
For example:
• 
 Ruled by the state government
• 
 All resources could be spent on the local 
community
Why it would be worse if our states and territories 
were like countries?
For example:
• 
 Specific laws
• 
 Taxes
• 
 Passports to move from one state or territory to 
another 
Explain to students that this is what Australia was like 
1788–1900. In 1901, Australia became one federated 
(united) country and the colonies joined together.
Objectives
• Understand why people wanted Australia to 
federate as one country
• Learn about the process of Federation in 
Australia
• Consider a positive outcome of Federation: 
female suffrage

ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
41
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Australian identity
Prior knowledge
A basic understanding of the history of Australia with 
a focus on the convict period, the early settlement, the 
gold rush and World War I would be helpful.
Background
Australia has had a relatively short period of time to 
develop its national identity, especially compared to 
other national images such as the English John Bull, 
or national characteristics such as the Germans being 
hardworking and the French being great lovers.
Of course, the Indigenous settlers of Australia had their 
own connection to the land as part of The Dreaming. 
However, given the diverse views, languages and 
customs of Indigenous Australian peoples, it is hard to 
determine how national this identity was before the 
Europeans took over. 
Initially, Australia was seen from a Eurocentric 
perspective. The land was rarely connected to 
the Indigenous Australian peoples. Instead, it was 
described in the legal terms terra nullius or ‘empty land’. 
This allowed the British to form their own Australian 
identity to replace the identity formed by Indigenous 
Australian peoples. 
The British first viewed Australia purely as a convict 
destination. This gave rise to a national identity shaped 
by the nature of those transported to the country: 
everyone was tainted with criminality. As settlement 
increased and images of Australia began to feature the 
unique bushland, the national image changed to that 
of the bushman. 
Over time, the national image changed twice more 
before 1918. First, the ‘working man’s paradise’ was 
a stark contrast to the working hell of England in 
the Industrial Revolution. Then the image focused 
on the Anzac ideals of manly mateship, camaraderie 
and larrikinism. This fitted the Australia forged on the 
fields of Gallipoli and the Western Front in World War I. 
Although powerful, these national images excluded 
numerous groups, particularly women, Indigenous 
Australian peoples and multicultural identities.
Starter activity
Ask the students to imagine that the whole country 
of Australia is a person, then draw a portrait of that 
person. Have them label their drawing to explain why 
they chose each feature and how it fits the national 
identity of Australia.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Ideas that shaped Australia’, 
presents the key ideas in the development of the 
Australian nation. It is paired with the Activity sheet, 
‘Exploring the ideas that shaped Australia’. Here, 
students match examples to the key ideas. Then 
they use at least three of these key ideas in a written 
description of Australia. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Australian identity’, provides an 
overview of Australia’s changing identity from the 
1780s until after 1914. 
Quote sources:
•  Miriam Dixson, The Real Matilda: Woman and Identity 
in Australia, 1788 to the Present, UNSW Press 1999, 
p.123
•  Russel Ward, The Australian Legend, Oxford University 
Press 1958, p.201
•  Jackie Hogan, Gender, Race and National Identity: 
Nations of Flesh and Blood, Routledge 2008 p.109
•  Graham Seal, Inventing Anzac: The Digger and National 
Mythology, University of Queensland Press 2004, p.4–6
In the Activity sheet, ‘Essay plan’, students are guided 
through the process of writing an essay plan using 
the information from the Resource sheet, ‘Australian 
identity’. As an extension activity, students are asked to 
use their plan to write an essay.
Extension ideas
Have students choose one of the identities explored 
in this unit (a national identity or one of the female 
identities) and create a piece of artwork to explore that 
identity. Ask the students to write several paragraphs or 
annotate a design plan to explain their artistic choices.
Objectives
• Learn about the changing nature of Australian 
identity, 1788–1918
• Consider how Australia defined itself
• Evaluate how the Australian identity has 
often excluded groups such as women and 
Indigenous Australian peoples

ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
49
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Cultural expression
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required.
Background
Australia has a long history of artwork – music, dance, 
film, photography and acting. The first Indigenous 
Australian peoples made cave paintings and dot 
paintings to record their stories, and performed dances 
and played music to explore their understanding of the 
world and their connection to it.
The settlement of Australia quickly led to European 
views of Australia, with many artists choosing to 
reframe Australia as a ‘New England’. Their artworks 
presented Australia in very English colours and tones. 
Some of the first settlers used their artistic skills to 
show the new settlements and even interactions with 
the Indigenous Australian peoples. At any state or 
national gallery in Australia, you can see the range of 
artwork moving from stereotypical English landscapes 
to a recognition of the wild desert bushland that 
was perhaps a more accurate representation of the 
Australia that the early settlers interacted with.
In the late 1800s, a number of writers and poets, such 
as Henry Lawson, Louisa Lawson, Banjo Paterson, Ethel 
Turner and Barcroft Henry Boake, helped to construct 
the Australian identity. Their vivid, descriptive writing 
contributed to a uniquely Australian identity rather 
than a colonial identity that was unique to each colony. 
These constructions of the Australian identity were one 
aspect of the push towards Federation in 1901 when 
Australia became one country. 
In the 1900s, Australia became a pioneer in the film 
industry. The Story of the Ned Kelly Gang was the 
first full-length film ever made. Australia became a 
powerful film industry player in the early years before 
Hollywood began dominating the scene. The Australian 
film industry only began to recover in the 1970s with 
funding from the federal and state governments.
Starter activity
Have the students create an artwork that represents 
their understanding of Australia. Discuss the different 
views revealed in the artworks.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Louisa Lawson and The Dawn’, 
introduces a significant Australian woman and her 
magazine, the first in Australia to be written for and by 
women. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Different views’, presents an 
illustration of an Indigenous Australian man. Students 
are asked to interpret the artist’s perspective on his 
subject before they create their own illustrations. 
The Resource sheet, ‘The Never Never’, has a poem by 
Barcroft Henry Boake. This is paired with the Activity 
sheet, ‘Deadly desert’. Here, students explore the 
powerful visual imagery of Boake’s poem. 
The Activity sheet, ‘The Story of the Ned Kelly Gang’, 
looks at the fledgling Australian film industry.
Extension ideas
Have students watch Youtube clips from the 1906 film 
The Story of the Kelly Gang. Note that only fragments of 
the film have survived. Then students could:
• 
recreate one scene and film or perform it
• 
write a review of the film
• 
 draw storyboards showing the style of filming of 
one key scene.
Objectives
• Learn about key cultural works in Australia in 
the 1800s and early 1900s
• Consider the impact of women on the 
development of Australian literature
• Understand the development of the film 
industry in Australia

ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
55
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Laws
Prior knowledge
A basic knowledge of Federation may be useful.
Background
With Federation in 1901, Australia became one country. 
Previously it had been a group of colonies existing in 
the same land, all with vastly differing laws, wages and 
cultures. 
Federation led to positive changes such as female 
suffrage. Australia was the first country in the world 
to allow women the right to vote and also to be 
represented in Parliament. New Zealand became the 
first country in the world to allow women to vote in 
1893. 
However, negative changes also resulted from 
Federation and they were linked firmly to racism. 
The increase in Chinese immigration during the 
gold rush and the location of Australia in the south-
east Asian region led to racist fears about an Asian 
invasion of Australia. There was a strong movement 
towards developing a White Australia. This was to be 
accomplished by preventing non-European and non-
white immigration through the Immigration Restriction 
Act of 1901. Within the country, Indigenous Australian 
people were mistreated because of those same racist 
ideas that made Europeans fear Asian immigration. 
The Australian Constitution was formulated in 1900 
and came into power in 1901. This document defined 
the rules and construction of Australian society, and 
the powers held federally and by the state. In the 
Constitution, Indigenous Australian people were 
excluded from the census, implying they did not exist. 
Their right to vote was also removed.
Starter activity
Lead a class discussion about laws. Ask students to 
think about some laws today that apply to teenagers. 
What is their purpose? Do you think they are fair or 
unfair? 
Focus the discussion on the issues of voting, 
immigration and family life, and in particular, how 
children’s lives are governed.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Immigration nation’, considers how 
different groups of migrants were treated in Australia. 
It is paired with the Activity sheet, ‘Immigration 
Restriction Act’, which explores the effects of this Act 
on immigration.
The Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous Australian people 
in 1901’, looks at how Indigenous Australians were 
included or excluded from voting and the census.
Extension ideas
Choose a group that moved to Australia from 
another country; for example: Chinese, Afghans, 
Pacific Islanders, Japanese or Irish.
• 
 Research when they came to Australia and create a 
timeline.
• 
 Why did choose Australia? Think of the advantages 
of living in Australia.
• 
 Why did they leave their own country? Think of the 
disadvantages of staying in that country. 
Objectives
• Learn about the Immigration Restriction Act of 
1901
• Consider the impact of removing the right of 
Indigenous Australian people to vote or to be 
counted in the census

ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
59
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Teacher’s notes – Money
Prior knowledge
A basic understanding of life in the 1900s in Australia 
will be useful.
Background
In the early 1900s, people changed the way they 
thought about the regulation of wages. Previously, the 
money paid to employees was determined entirely by 
the employer. Wages were set to benefit the employer, 
not the employed. 
As the self-described egalitarian nation, Australia 
wanted to form a society where all people were 
equal. However, their understanding of equality 
regularly excluded women, non-European migrants 
and Indigenous Australian people. The theory of 
egalitarianism was a positive image of a welcoming, 
open country, but the reality was less positive. The 
image of equality applied to all white men. Unlike 
Britain, it was to be a classless society – though still, of 
course, a racist and sexist one.
After Federation in 1901, Australia worked towards 
establishing a pension to support the care of those 
over the age of 65 years. This happened in 1908. To 
be eligible for a pension, people had to have lived 
in Australia for more than 25 years and be of good 
character. This meant that the government had some 
control over the behaviour of those people who 
wanted the pension. They had to prove their moral 
worth, which reinforced the notion of Australia as 
egalitarian but also superior to other countries. 
Interestingly, the maternity allowance introduced 
in 1912 had no similar ‘good character’ clause. All 
mothers, whether of legitimate or illegitimate children, 
were entitled to claim the five pound bonus. This was 
probably intended to protect the health and expansion 
of the future Australian population rather than support 
unwed mothers.
Starter activity
Use the trove website (http://trove.nla.gov.au) to help 
you identify five items that most people bought in the 
1910s and still use today. Find out how much each one 
cost in 1910. Then use an online supermarket website 
to find out how much these items cost today.
• 
How much has the cost of each item changed?
• 
Why do you think it has changed?
• 
 Which item has changed the most? 
Remember:  £1 (one pound) = 20s (twelve shillings) 
1s (one shilling) = 12d (12 pennies)
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Minimum wage’, identifies two key 
legal cases that contributed to the minimum wage: 
the Harvester Judgement and the Fruit Pickers Case. 
Students will use this Activity sheet to help them 
complete the Activity sheet, ‘Impact on Australia’. Here, 
students apply their knowledge to writing speeches 
that express conflicting points of view. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Pensions and maternity allowance’ 
looks at the introduction of two key forms of economic 
support for marginalised groups. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Food and money’, outlines the 
costs of living in 1911 and 1915. It accompanies the 
Activity sheet, ‘Comparing costs’, where students 
analyse how costs changed over these four years.
Extension ideas
• 
 Ask students to work in pairs or small groups 
to create a weekly meal plan for a family: wife, 
husband and three children. Students should use 
the food listed on the Activity sheet, ‘Food and 
money’. 
 
 Hint: Remember that in the 1910s, food was British 
in style; for example, meat and three vegetables, 
roasts, bread and pies. 
• 
 Students could then use their meal plans and the 
prices from the Resource sheet, ‘Food and money’, 
to make a budget for life in 1915. They should 
include all food costs and rent, plus matches, wood 
and kerosene which were used to both light and 
heat houses. Total weekly spending should be 
under £3 2s.
Objectives
• Learn about the impacts of the Harvester 
Judgement and Fruit Pickers Case on 
establishing the minimum wage
• Gain an understanding of the economic 
situation by creating meal plans
• Consider the introduction of pensions and 
maternity allowances on the development of 
Australia

Indigenous Australians and their land
Terra nullius is a Latin term that means ‘empty land’. The British used terra nullius as a legal 
excuse for invading Australia. Because Indigenous Australian peoples were not settling and 
farming the land in the same ways that Europeans did, the British simply took over by settling 
first in Sydney Cove and, later, in other parts of Australia. 
+ 
1  Complete these sentences.
 
a 
Terra nullius means  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
b 
British settlers used this term because  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
It is hard to know exactly how many Indigenous people lived in Australia before 1788 because 
they didn’t keep written records of their populations, and many died after colonisation. Some 
historians believe there were 750,000 Indigenous Australians speaking 300–700 languages. In 
many ways, Indigenous Australia was like a continent of many countries, not just one country.
2 How many Indigenous Australians were there before 1788?  
 
 
3 How many different Indigenous Australian languages were there?  
 
 
 
4 What do you think life in Australia was like before European settlement?
 
 
 
 
Indigenous Australians didn’t produce food in the ways that Europeans were used to. Groups 
hunted and gathered food or trapped animals using techniques such as ‘fire-stick farming’. 
This involved setting fire to areas so kangaroos could use the land for grazing and travelling. 
Hunters used sophisticated tools and trapping techniques to gather the meat they needed. 
Some groups used techniques that Europeans recognise as agriculture. The Wiradjuri in 
New South Wales collected the grains of millet grasses to make bread, and the Gunditjmara in 
Victoria built a series of canals and fences to farm eels.
5 What farming techniques have Indigenous Australian people used?

Penal colony or pastoral settlement
Britain colonised Australia to use it as a place for British criminals to serve their sentences. 
Over time, European settlers saw the possibilities in growing crops and raising stock. These 
first settlements were often called pastoral settlements because most had sheep and cattle. 
Pastoral means using land for the grazing of sheep and cows.  
New South Wales was the first area settled. Originally this colony covered half of Australia. The 
other half was called New Holland. Over time, these colonies became the states and territories 
we know today: Victoria, New South Wales, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania, 
Queensland and Northern Territory.

ACHIEVE!   History: Making a nation – Australia, 1750–1918
11
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2017
Activity sheet – Indigenous Australian peoples
Prior knowledge
Students need a basic understanding of the settlement 
of Australia.
Background
The treatment of Indigenous Australian people by the 
European settlers was often problematic. It was rare 
that the two groups made treaties. The treaty John 
Batman made in Victoria in 1835 with the Wurundjeri 
Elders may be the only one of its kind in Australia. 
The settlers’ permanent usage of land destroyed the 
semi-nomadic lifestyles of the Indigenous Australian 
peoples. Settlement in Victoria was quicker than 
in other states as the land was so flat, unlike New 
South Wales with the mountains beyond Sydney, or 
South Australia with the swamps around Adelaide. 
Indigenous Australian peoples struggled to survive 
after their lands were taken away. They suffered from 
the introduction of diseases like influenza and smallpox 
and the massacres, violence and sexual attacks from 
settlers. 
In some areas Indigenous Australian people fought 
back, like the Wiradjuri in the Blue Mountains. In 
other places like Coranderrk, an Aboriginal Reserve 
in Victoria, Indigenous Australians responded by 
following European methods of dispute resolution: 
petitions, deputations and court hearings. 
The European settlers often had negative views about 
the Indigenous Australian peoples, seeing them initially 
as ‘vermin’, and later as a ‘dying race’. Some people felt 
that ‘half-caste’* children (children of both Indigenous 
Australian and European parentage) should be 
removed from their homes and raised in reserves and 
missions. Often this was done by religious or charity 
groups. The intention was to assimilate these children 
into the white community. Members of these Stolen 
Generations often experienced physical and sexual 
abuse and treatment as second class citizens, as well as 
the loss of family and culture. 
Starter activity
Ask the students to work in small groups to make a 
Venn diagram comparing:
• 
Indigenous Australian life before settlement (1700s)
• 
 Indigenous Australian life in the first years of 
European settlement (1800s–1850s). 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘The treatment of Indigenous 
Australians’, explores the conflict between the 
Wiradjuri people and Europeans in New South Wales. 
This concept is further explored in the Activity sheet, 
‘Coranderrk’, which outlines issues between settlers 
and the Wurundjeri people in Victoria.
The Activity sheet, ‘History wars’, provides an overview 
of two key issues historians have with Indigenous 
Australian history: the validity of oral history and 
focusing on positive or negative events.
The Resource sheet, ‘Stolen Generations’, gives 
information about the Stolen Generations through 
speech bubbles. People with a first and last name are 
real people, with text referring to their lives. People 
with initials as surnames are fictionalised characters 
whose dialogue is based on historical facts.
It is paired with the Activity sheet, ‘Perspectives on the 
Stolen Generations’, where students consider the views 
and aims of different groups.
Extension ideas
Have students further research Coranderrk and the 
difficulties faced in the first fights for Indigenous 
Australian civil rights. Useful websites:
http://ergo.slv.vic.gov.au/explore-history/fight-rights/
indigenous-rights/coranderrk-mission
http://coranderrk.com/
http://www.minutesofevidence.com.au/the-
coranderrk-story/
Objectives
• Learn about the experiences of the Indigenous 
peoples of Australia
• Consider how European colonists and 
Indigenous peoples interacted
• Identify key events that impacted on the 
development of Australia such as the Stolen 
Generations and the settlement at Coranderrk
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.
* Make sure students understand that ‘half-caste’ is 
a historical term and very much outdated in usage. 
Today, it is highly offensive, especially to Indigenous 
Australian peoples. It is linked to the historical belief 
that people of different racial groups should not

Stolen Generations
My mum didn’t want 
them to take me, but 
she didn’t have a choice. 
T he Aboriginal Board 
sent police for me and 
I couldn’t ever go home 
again. I have to go to 
school and I get hit if I 
don’t speak English. Some 
of them have done bad 
things to me. But nobody 
listens to an Aboriginal girl.
T he Native Welfare lady came 
by our camp. I saw her looking 
at my daughter Joyce. I told 
Joyce, ‘You’ll have to run or 
they’ll catch you up. And if they 
grab you they’ll never let you go.’ 
I was lucky. She ran and ran. 
And when the Native Welfare 
lady left, we moved to a 
dif ferent station. Later I heard 
that lady came back and took 
two other kids from our camp.
Ada Injie, 1930s
Auber Neville, 
Chief Protector 
of Aborigines in 
Western Australia, 
1930s
To leave half-caste* Aboriginal children 
with their parents is not good for them 
or their parents. It is only by removing 
children from the parents and taking 
them to missions that we can uplift the 
Native race. 
I believe that their new situation in the 
missions is far more satisfactory than 
the living conditions that they resided in 
before and no-one can convince me that 
I am wrong in this matter. 
Full-blooded* Aborigines will surely become 
extinct soon and if we don’t help the 
half-castes*, the same thing will happen 
to them.
I was taken from my mum to live 
in a dormitory on the mission. T he 
older kids used to tell me stories 
of when this country was our land 
but I try not to think about it. 
I mean, I’m thirteen – I’ll be 
working next year.
* The terms ‘half-caste’ and ‘full-blooded’ were once 
commonly used. Today, they are highly offensive, especially 
to Indigenous Australian peoples. These terms are linked 
to the historical belief that people of different racial groups 
should not marry nor have children – a racist idea that is 
considered completely unacceptable in today’s society.

Activity sheet – Non-European immigration
Chinese immigration
+ Copy and complete the sentences in the right column in your workbook.
The first Chinese migrants to Australia were sailors 
who left their ships and became cheap labourers. 
However, large numbers of Chinese immigrants came 
for the gold rush in the 1850s. They called Australia 
‘New Gold Mountain’. Most of these immigrants 
planned to stay long enough to make their fortunes 
and then go home. 
1  Most Chinese immigrants 
came to Australia because 
____.
Most gold rush migrants went to country towns like 
Ballarat and Bendigo. The Chinese miners sometimes 
created secret groups to establish rules and punish 
rule-breakers. This allowed them to maintain a good 
reputation and keep safe. 
2  Chinese miners created 
secret societies because ___.
There was a lot of racism in early Australia and many 
Chinese people were treated badly. In the 1850s, 
Victoria and South Australia put restrictions on the 
number of Chinese who could enter the colony. 
3  Events in the 1800s that 
showed racist attitudes 
include ____.
In 1861, there were riots at the Lambing Flat gold 
mines in New South Wales. European miners attacked 
the Chinese camps. Most Chinese miners lost all their 
belongings. Many were severely injured and some 
had their pigtails cut off. European miners had always 
treated Chinese miners badly, but the size, planning 
and violence of this attack was something new.
4  Lambing Flat was important 
because ____.
In 1901 there were 29,000 Chinese people living 
in Australia. This was the year of Federation, when 
the six colonies became one country. One of the 
first Acts of the new Australian Government was 
the Immigration Restriction Act of 1901. This law was 
used to restrict non-European immigration and this 
continued until the 1970s.
5  Three examples of racism in 
our society today are ____.

Racism in Australia
+ 
 Use the Resource sheet, ‘Mongolian Octopus’, to complete the source 
analysis below. It is based on the CHIPS structure. Discuss each question 
with a partner and write your own answer in your workbook.
1 Caption
 
a 
The text at the left of the image is the caption. What does it tell you?
 
b 
 How does the caption help us understand the image? For example, 
Mongolian Octopus: the word Mongolian was often used to describe all 
Asian people and could be seen as an insult.
2 Historical connections
 
a 
When was this image created?
 
b 
What events and issues were happening in this time?
 
c 
How does the image connect to the time period?
3 Interrogate the image
 
a 
What stands out in the image? Why?
 
b 
What is unusual about this image?
 
c 
 What is absent that should be shown? What is present that shouldn’t be? 
For example, it is rare to see pictures of white and black students together 
in schools before the 1950s in America because of segregation. So a 
photo showing black and white students together would be important.
4 People
 
a 
Who is in the image? Why? 
 
b 
 Are these figures represented positively or negatively? How can you tell? 
Why are they presented that way?
5 Signs and Symbols
 
a 
 What symbols are used? For example, a flag represents a country. 
An octopus represents something greedy and grasping.
 
b 
What are these symbols being used to say?

Octopus’, to write your own paragraph responding to the image.

Activity sheet – Non-European immigration
Blackbirding
In Queensland, many of the first settlers started up large farms called plantations. Most grew 
sugar cane. These plantations were so large that the settlers could not harvest all the sugar 
cane by themselves, so they brought people from the Pacific Islands to work as cheap labour. 
‘Blackbirding’ was the term for ‘convincing’ Pacific Islanders to come to Australia. Over 60,000 
people were ‘blackbirded’ during the 1800s.
Pacific Islanders were often:
•  kidnapped or tricked into going to Queensland
•  lied to about how much money they would earn
•  called ‘Kanakas’, a negative term
•  paid very little
•  given three year contracts they could not escape
•  made to work very long hours in harsh conditions.
I was the founder of Townsville 
in Queensland, and one of the 
first shipowners to bring Pacific 
Islanders to Australia to work in 
the sugar fields. T hey make good 
workers and I get to make good 
money. Black people are better 
workers than white people – they 
can deal better with the heat.
Robert Towns, 1840s
+ 
1   Use the information above to write a diary entry about your life as a ‘sugar slave’. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2  Imagine that you are a Queensland plantation owner.  
Explain why you need ‘Kanaka’ labour.
 
 
 
 
3 How else could the plantation owners solve their labour problem?

Sanitation and health
Bathrooms were very different for the rich and the poor during the 1900s in Australia.
Rich people
Poor people
Many homes had flushable 
toilets. Mass production of 
these began in the 1850s in 
England.
Many had bathrooms with 
porcelain bath tubs. They 
could wash regularly.
Most had taps in their houses 
giving them easy access to 
water.
Most people used outside dunnies as toilets. Nightsoil 
men would collect the waste at night. 
Some used cesspits as toilets. These were large holes that 
people used until they were filled.
Most used tin tubs to wash in and the whole family would 
share the same water. It was not done often, as it was 
hard to heat the water and they could not keep it warm.
Most people didn’t have taps in their houses. They used 
common wells or taps in public areas and carried the 
water back to their homes.

Homes
Houses in the 1900s were very different to houses today. They were often a lot smaller, with 
simpler technology and far less furniture. Houses built for middle class or wealthy people 
between 1900 and 1910 were often called Edwardian. They had high sloping roofs and were 
made of red brick or a pale weatherboard.
In 1900, a worker’s cottage in Melbourne or 
Sydney cost about five shillings (sixty cents)  
a week to rent. They had two rooms: a 
kitchen and a bedroom. The toilet was 
usually an outside closet.
+

Working class men, women and children
The lives of unskilled workers were often hard in Australia in the 1900s. Although there were 
many changes in technology and lifestyle, the lives of the poorest people were similar to those 
100 years earlier.
T he roads are often covered in 
sewage. I have to be careful 
where I step so I don’t get 
covered in the muck. Nobody 
wants to buy things from someone 
who smells like the streets.
I never used to work. 
T hen my man got sick and 
I started working for 
Mr Taylor at the clothes 
factory. At first I took 
cloth home and hemmed it 
because it was easier with 
the children. But it didn’t 
pay much and in the end 
I went to the factory. 
T he hours are long, but we 
have to eat.
T hey call Australia a working man’s 
paradise. Maybe it used to be 
before but not now in 1900. I live 
near my factory. T here are only a 
few trams and buses so I usually 
walk. Sometimes I think of moving 
to the country where the air is 
clear and a man could be himself. 
James T., 38 years
Simone L., 23 years
Maddie M., 13 years
My friend Maddie still goes to 
school, but I didn’t see the point. 
I started working in a factory a 
year ago, even though you aren’t 
supposed to until you are fifteen. 
If a truant of ficer turns up, we lie 
and say we are older. I got made 
an apprentice at first and I earned 
nothing for the first six months.
Shelby L., 
14 years
Reuben J., 28 years
My mother sends me to 
school. She wants me 
to learn well and become 
a teacher. T he money 
for teaching is better 
than other jobs. And if 
I get to be a governess, 
I might meet a rich man 
to marry.

Resource sheet – Federation
Colony to country
When Australia was claimed by the British, they divided Australia into six separate colonies: 
Western Australia, South Australia which controlled Northern Territory, New South Wales, 
Victoria, Queensland and Tasmania.
Colonies like New South Wales and Victoria were right next to each other and yet each had very 
different laws and taxes. By the late 1800s, many people saw themselves more as Australians 
than as Victorians or Tasmanians. They wanted the colonies to federate and become one 
country. In 1901, Australia finally became a Federation.

Suffragettes
The word suffrage means the right to vote. Before the 19th century, only rich men could vote 
for political leaders. Slowly, things began to change.

1850s: Groups like the 
Chartists campaigned for 
suffrage for all men. 
1880s: Many men got the 
right to vote.
1880s: Many women began 
fighting for the right to vote. 
These women were called 
suffragettes. They knew that 
without the right to vote, 
politicians would not care 
about them and their needs. 
Many different suffrage 
societies were formed to help 
women get the vote.
1884: Henrietta Dugdale 
helped found the Victorian 
Women’s Suffrage Society. 
She was a famous Australian 
suffragette and wrote a novel 
about living in a future where 
men and women are equal. 
1885: The Women’s Christian 
Temperance Union (WCTU) 
was formed in Sydney. 
Their main purpose was to 
fight against alcohol. They 
campaigned for female 
suffrage so that they could 
vote on alcohol laws. 
1891: Vida Goldstein led 
women of Victoria to create 
a ‘monster petition’. It was 
260 metres long and signed 
by 30,000 people, all asking 
for women to have the right 
to vote.
1895: South Australia 
became the first colony to 
allow all women, including 
Indigenous Australians, 
to vote. 
1902: Australia introduced 
female suffrage, becoming 
the first place in the world to 
allow women to both vote and 
be represented in parliament. 
However, the right for 
Indigenous Australians to vote 
was not included. 
1967: A Referendum allowed 
Indigenous Australians 
to vote.

Healthy nation
Sickness – 1890s to 1910s
•  Poor sanitation or water use 
made it easy for diseases to 
spread.
•  Many babies died from 
diseases like cholera and 
typhus.
•  In January 1900, there was 
an outbreak of the bubonic 
plague in Sydney. There 
were 12 other outbreaks 
between 1900 and 1920.
Health – 1890s to 1910s
Attitudes towards health changed during this time.
•  Health experts visited homes to give advice.
•  Quarantine standards changed.
•  Changes to sanitation meant that fewer 
children died. 
•  Doctors studied diseases to find cures. 
Australian doctors John Thompson, William 
Armstrong and Frank Tidswell studied the bubonic 
plague. They finally concluded that it was the fleas on 
rats that spread the disease.
+  1 Describe how animals and water caused disease and death during this time.

2 List two things doctors did to improve health conditions.
 
 
3 Name three common diseases of the time. 
 
 
4  Imagine you are the Minister for Health in the Australian Government. Choose one 
health issue and outline how you would solve it.
 
 
 
 
 
 
5  Imagine you are the parent of a sick child in 1910. In your workbook, write a paragraph 
about what your child’s illness is, how your child became sick and how changing 
attitudes towards health saved your child.

Topic sentence (Introduces your body paragraph) – When Australia was first settled by the 
Europeans it was seen as a penal colony, which led to the idea of Australia as a convict 
destination.
What was Australia’s identity? Why did it have that identity?
Evidence – We had convicts at the beginning of Australia’s history.

how it was seen.
How did that shape how Australia was seen?
Evidence – ‘Convicts… evoked widespread revulsion’. Many people ‘felt horror and fear 
about them.’ Miriam Dixson

way Australia was seen.
Evidence – Australian women were seen as prostitutes. 
Explain – Convict women were often seen as prostitutes or sexually immoral. Over time, all 
Australian women began to be seen in this negative light. 
Mini-conclusion (sums up your body paragraph)  – Australia’s initial identity was associated 
with convicts, as they were the first Europeans sent to Australia, shaping the nation as a 
home for criminals.

Louisa Lawson and The Dawn
Louisa Lawson was a writer, editor and publisher. She was one of the first women in Australia 
to start a magazine that was written for women, by women. She called her magazine The Dawn 
and began publishing it in 1888. The first issue of the magazine included an editorial where 
Louisa wrote: 
“Here we will give publicity to women’s wrongs, will fight their battles, assist to repair what evils 
we can, and give advice to the best of our ability.”
Louisa was also a suffragette and fought for the right of female suffrage, which means the right 
to vote. She fought for women’s rights in general: 
• promoting the idea that married women should be allowed to work outside of the home
• suggesting there should be childcare facilities to help women work 
• employing women writers and printers at The Dawn
• fighting unions that wanted her to employ only men. 
Despite all Louisa’s accomplishments, she is mainly remembered as the mother of writer 
Henry Lawson.   
+ 
1  What do you believe is Louisa Lawson’s most important accomplishment? 
Explain why.
 
 
 
 
2  Louisa is remembered as the mother of a writer and not as a writer herself. What does 
this tell you about the world that women lived in at that time?
 
 
 
 
3 Why was The Dawn so important?
 
 
 
 
4  In your workbook, write an obituary for Louisa Lawson. An obituary is a record of the 
important parts of someone’s life. It is published soon after they die.

The Never Never
Barcroft Henry Boake was an Australian bush poet. He wrote many poems in 1890–91 while 
trying to find a job during the Depression. He died in 1892. His famous poem Where the dead 
men lie describes the Australian outback. Here is an excerpt from it.
 
Glossary
bleach: turn white from the sun, over time
heat-waves: when it has been really hot for 
a long time and the air looks wavy
mated: married
Never Never: outback Australia
pinions: wing feathers of a bird
saltbush: a plant that can live in the desert
tryst: romantic relationship, usually with a 
boyfriend or girlfriend
unsated: unsatisfied
FA Sleap (engraver) and J Macfarlane (artist), The stony desert – Sturt's third expedition, 
1891, State Library of Victoria, IAN01/01/91/supp/5.
Where the dead men lie
Out on the wastes of the Never Never— 
   That’s where the dead men lie! 
There where the heat-waves dance for ever— 
   That’s where the dead men lie! 
That’s where the Earth’s loved sons are keeping 
Endless tryst: not the west wind sweeping 
Feverish pinions, can wake their sleeping— 
   Out where the dead men lie!
Where brown Summer and Death have mated— 
   That’s where the dead men lie! 
Loving with fiery lust unsated— 
   That’s where the dead men lie! 
Out where the grinning skulls bleach whitely 
Under the saltbush sparkling brightly; 
Out where the wild dogs chorus nightly— 
   That’s where the dead men lie!

Immigration nation

Activity sheet – Laws
Immigration Restriction Act
In 1901, fears about different racial groups led to the Australian Government passing the 
Immigration Restriction Act. This was one of the first Acts of the new Australian Government.
It meant that people were only allowed to come to Australia if they:
•  could write a passage of 50 words dictated in any European language
•  could support themselves financially
•  didn’t suffer from mental illness or infectious disease
•  were not prostitutes or criminals.
This policy became known as the White Australia policy. Although it did not mention any racial 
group in particular, it was mostly used to restrict non-white immigration to Australia.
+ 
1  What do you think about this immigration policy? Include reasons for your 
answer. You could use the word bank for ideas. 
Word bank:  discriminate, unfair, equality, racism, white, black, persecute, sexism, 
reasons, separate, differentiate, decisions, choices
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
In the 1950s, the Minister for Immigration relaxed the White Australia policy. Japanese war 
brides and a wider range of refugees from eastern European countries such as Lithuania, 
Latvia and the Soviet Union were allowed to immigrate. After the Vietnam War in the 1970s, 
Vietnamese boat people were welcomed into Australia, finally ending the Immigration 
Restriction Act. 
2  Work with a partner. In your workbook, make a list of countries from which people 
migrate to Australia today. Why do you think these groups come to Australia? Consider 
ideas about work, persecution, family, war and work skills.

Indigenous Australian people in 1901
Before 1901, the rights of Indigenous Australian people were restricted by the laws of the 
colony they lived in. This meant that although Indigenous Australian men and women 
were allowed to vote in South Australia in 1894, the right to vote was denied to those from 
Queensland in 1885 and West Australians from 1893. 
In the late 1890s, people began discussing the idea of making the separate colonies into a 
single country: Australia. At the same time there was a focus on creating a white Australia. 
In 1901 when every other man and woman in Australia was given the right to vote, Indigenous 
Australian people were excluded. Even in states like South Australia where they had been given 
the vote, it was taken away.  
+ 
1  Highlight the underlined text that would have a positive effect on Indigenous 
Australian people. Then circle the underlined text that would have a negative 
effect on Indigenous Australian people. 
2  Summarise how Indigenous Australians were treated by the law before 1901.
 
 
 
 
In 1901, the government held a national census to help them gain a better understanding of 
the population of Australia and the needs of Australians. 
The Australian Constitution became law on Federation in 1901. When the constitution was 
being formed, it was decided that Indigenous Australian people would not be counted in the 
census. This decision was only repealed in 1967.
Section 127 (now repealed) of the Constitution said:

Harvester Judgement
In 1907, Justice Higgins was the judge in a case about 
wages. He had to decide what a fair wage for a worker 
was. Justice Higgins decided that the minimum wage 
should be seven shillings (7s) a day for unskilled 
workers. This was seen as a ‘family wage’ – the money 
needed to support a husband, wife and two children.
His decision in this case helped to create the 
minimum wage for men in Australia. The case was 
called the ‘Harvester Judgement’.

Fruit Pickers Case
The minimum wage of the Harvester Judgement only 
applied to men. But women worked as well, even

Women were often paid as little as their employer 
could get away with. Justice Higgins decided that 
women did not need a family wage as women should 
not be supporting a family. All families should have 
a man working to support them. Women were paid 
about half of the male wage.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
5
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Who were the Vikings?
Objectives
l	 Identify how the legend of the Vikings 
continues to permeate and influence the 
modern world
l	 Recognise relevant geographical locations 
and situate Europe – and in particular, 
Scandinavia – on a world map
l	 Identify the geographical spread of Viking 
influence 
Prior knowledge
Students should have some basic map-reading 
skills and be able to identify at least their home 
country in an atlas. 
Background
The Vikings were a legendary people and, as such, 
the potential for misconceptions about who they 
were and how they lived is considerable. They came 
from Scandinavia, travelled throughout Europe and 
beyond, and dominated Europe from the late 8th 
to the 11th centuries. ‘Who were the Vikings?’ aims 
to clarify when the Vikings lived, where they came 
from and how far their influence spread, and to get 
students thinking about their own assumptions and 
how these are shaped. 
Starter activity
Ask students to pair up and, working with their 
partner, draw how they think a Viking looked. Ensure 
that students know that they do not need to worry 
about whether or not their representation is correct. 
Once everyone has drawn their Viking, invite each 
pair to share their picture with the class. On the 
board, make a list of any features that the pictures 
had in common. For example, how common were 
horned helmets? Are students aware that Vikings 
did not have horns on their helmets? From here, it is 
ideal to move straight on to the first Activity sheet 
‘Pop quiz – legendary Vikings’. 
Resource and Activity sheets
As a class, read the Activity sheet ‘Pop quiz – legendary 
Vikings’. Ask the students to write their answers 
individually, and then discuss the answers as a class.  
The aim is to generate discussion about the assumptions 
we make about the Vikings, as well as about other 
peoples and historic events. Discuss the use of reliable 
sources such as school texts, educational internet sites 
and documentaries. Remind students that ‘CE’ stands 
for ‘Common Era’.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘The Viking 
Age’ before reading and completing the Activity sheet 
‘The Vikings travel far and wide’. Discuss the information 
in both sheets. Ensure that students understand where 
Scandinavia is in relation to where the students live. 
Students can then use the information they have 
gathered in both these sheets to complete the Activity 
sheet ‘Vikings’.
Finally, students can complete the Activity sheet 
‘Tracking the Vikings’. This sheet emphasises how far the 
Vikings travelled and their scope of influence. 
Extension activity
As a class, discuss the importance of how extensively 
the Vikings dominated Europe. Using an atlas, work out 
how far it is from Sweden to Spain. You will need to use 
the map scale to calculate this. Put this distance into a 
context the students can comprehend – for example, 
from their school to another city. How hard would it 
have been for the Vikings to cover that distance? How 
would students cover that distance without cars? 
Would climate have been a big factor for the Vikings? 
Remember, northern Europe is very cold and the seas 
can be very rough.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
11
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – A harsh existence
Objectives
l	 Recognise and identify the main topographical 
features of Scandinavia
l	 Examine how climate and topography 
influenced the Viking way of life 
l	 Develop an understanding of ordinary 
Viking life
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic understanding of 
what ‘topography’ means and why it matters, 
particularly the fact that it may hamper movement 
between regions.
Background
Scandinavia is comprised of Norway, Sweden and 
Denmark. Each country has its own topographical 
features and climatic hurdles, all of which combined 
to make living in Scandinavia hard. It is believed 
that the Vikings originally journeyed out of 
Scandinavia in search of resources and a better way 
of life. The Vikings, while known for their fierce raids 
and extensive travels, generally lived very simple, 
hard lives. 
Starter activity
Discuss with students what topography is and 
how both it and climate can affect the way people 
live. Get students to think about and describe the 
topography of their local area. Is it hilly or flat? What 
is the climate like? Imagine life without cars and 
electricity. How would the local topography and 
climate affect the way the students live? Also, use 
this activity as an opportunity to introduce students 
to the concept of a fjord. Have them search the 
internet for images and definitions of fjords. Discuss 
these findings as a class. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Mountains, 
plains and lots of water’ before completing the 
Activity sheet ‘Scandinavian topography’. Both these 
sheets encourage students to consider the effect of 
topography on lifestyle.
Students can complete the Activity sheet 
‘Scandinavian climate’, then, in pairs, they can work  
on completing the Activity sheet ‘How does 
Scandinavia’s climate compare to mine?’. Students are 
invited to compare their own lifestyle and climate to 
that of the Vikings. This helps develop understanding 
and empathy. Students will need to research the climate 
in their area. Direct them to www.weatherzone.com.au 
or www.eldersweather.com.au for highest and lowest 
recorded temperatures and sunset and sunrise times.
Students can complete the final Activity sheet 
in the unit, ‘A day in the life of a Viking’, individually. 
Take some time initially to discuss with students what 
a synonym is. Provide them with examples of common 
synonyms, such as ‘beautiful’ and ‘pretty’.   
Extension activity
What does your seasonal year look like? As a class, 
list the sorts of things students do in each season. 
Are there activities or foods they look forward to – or 
prefer to avoid – in each season? How might this 
compare with the Viking year? For example, winter 
would mean scarce food production and icy cold 
conditions. 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.subject: History

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
17
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Farming and raiding 
Objectives
l	 Understand that Vikings were first and 
foremost farmers 
l	 Recognise the role of dwindling resources on 
the Vikings’ decision to move further out of 
Scandinavia 
l	 Consider the importance of raiding to the 
dominance of the Vikings
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of where 
Scandinavia is and the difficulties inherent in living 
there. They should also have some concept of how 
far the Vikings managed to travel from Scandinavia. 
Background
Most Vikings were farmers. Even those Vikings 
who left Scandinavia in search of better resources 
ended up living simple, farm-based lives in their 
new lands. 
The raids for which the Vikings became 
legendary were well planned, swift and fierce. The 
dominance of Vikings throughout Europe during 
the Viking Age is due in no small part to their 
effectiveness as warriors, the speed and scope of 
their exploits and the fact that they were feared by 
many people. 
Starter activity
As a class, discuss the assumptions we make about 
people depending on how they live. For example, 
how would we tend to describe the people who 
live in peasant, farming societies? List on the board 
the sorts of words we might use to describe their 
characters. How would we describe the people who 
live in warrior societies, where fighting is considered 
important? List these words on the board too. 
The Vikings were both farmers and warriors. Are 
our assumptions sometimes too simplistic? How 
important is it to have an open mind when studying 
history and other cultures?
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Viking farmers’ 
and then complete the Activity sheet ‘Then and now’. 
Encourage students to imagine the life of a Viking 
farmer and to consider how much easier our lives are 
today because of modern technology.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Away on 
a Viking raid’ as a class. They can then complete 
the Activity sheet ‘To raid or not to raid?’. After this, 
everyone’s results can be shared with the rest of the 
class to prompt discussion about the complexities 
of raiding.
Finally, students can complete the Activity sheet 
‘Help plan a raid’. Some students may require assistance 
with sequencing. You might choose to do the 
sequencing as a class and then let students draw their 
own pictures in their workbooks individually.  
Extension activity
Divide the class into three groups. One group will argue 
that raiding is important and necessary. Another will 
argue that raiding is barbaric and unnecessary. The 
third group will adjudicate and determine which side 
has the most convincing case. Give the first two groups 
five minutes to prepare their arguments, and then four 
minutes each to present their case. While the arguing 
sides compose their arguments, the adjudicating group 
can develop a marking scheme to help them decide 
which side wins the debate.

uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.subject: History
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.description: Vikings and the Medieval World. Teaching Guide.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
23
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Social structure and honour 
Objectives
l	 Identify the three main Viking social classes
l	 Recognise the importance of honour in Viking 
culture
l	 Explore the role of Viking women in Viking 
society 
l	 Introduce students to ‘things’ as a form of 
governance
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge required.
Background
Viking society was very ordered. There were clear 
class delineations and laws were strictly enforced. 
Honour was central to Viking culture. Roles and 
responsibilities were divided between men and 
women. For example, women took care of all 
matters related to the home and family, while men 
looked after the farms, boats and trade. However, 
when the men went away on long trips, the women 
were left in charge of everything. While not having 
as many rights as Viking men, Viking women 
certainly fared better than women in other parts of 
Europe at the time. 
Starter activity 
Discuss as a class how ‘outsiders’ might view our 
society. Imagine that a group of aliens were to come 
here. How would you describe our society to them? 
What would you say about the roles of men and 
women? How important are children in our society? 
What are the values that underpin our society? Do 
we have a class system? What does it look like?
Resource and Activity sheets
As a class, read the Resource sheet ‘Viking hierarchy’. 
Write the names of the social classes on the board and 
discuss the differences between them. Some students 
may need help pronouncing the class names and 
understanding the differences between the classes. 
Students can then complete the Activity sheet ‘In 
their place’.
After students have completed the Activity sheet 
‘The role of Viking women’, discuss as a class how 
women’s roles have changed since the Viking Age.
Before students attempt the Activity sheet ‘Honour’, 
spend some time discussing what honour means. 
The Activity sheet ‘Things – Viking meetings’ invites 
students to compare modern governments to the 
Viking meetings called ‘things’.
Extension activity
Honour was central to Viking life and society. As a 
class, create a definition of honour that is relevant to 
contemporary society. For example, behaving with 
honour is behaving in a way that respects yourself 
and other people; it can include sticking by your 
friends, not telling lies and taking responsibility for 
your actions. 
Is honour considered as important in our society 
today? Are there other personal characteristics or 
behaviours that are considered more important than 
honour in our society? Make a list. Can students think of 
how (through our behaviour, customs or social systems) 
we as a society reinforce the importance of these 
personal characteristics?

uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.title: The Vikings - A seafaring people
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.subject: History
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.description: Vikings and the Medieval World. Teaching Guide.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
29
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – A seafaring people 
Objectives
l	 Recognise that the dominance exerted by 
the Vikings was due largely to their skills as 
boatbuilders and sailors
l	 Identify the main features of Viking boats 
(e.g. shallow hull, symmetrical design, single 
large sail) 
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of where 
Scandinavia is located and of the extensive bodies 
of water the Vikings had to navigate. 
Background
Much of the widespread influence and dominance 
of the Vikings can be attributed to their prowess as 
boatbuilders, sailors and navigators. They had the 
most extensive fleets of their time, and their ability 
to swiftly sneak up on unsuspecting villages and 
cities by way of sea routes was second to none. 
Starter activity
As a class, brainstorm all the current modes of 
transport used by human beings. If one country 
was to try to dominate as many other countries 
as possible and they could only use one mode of 
transport to do it, which mode of transport would 
they would pick? Why? 
Explain to students that during the Viking Age 
the most advanced and swiftest mode of transport 
was the boat. The society that built the largest 
and fastest boats would be able to dominate 
through war and trade. The Vikings were the best 
boatbuilders and sailors of their time.
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can complete the Activity sheet ‘The Vikings 
and their boats’ with a partner. This sheet introduces 
students to the three main types of Viking sea craft. 
Students could then read the Resource sheet 
‘Viking longships 1’ before attempting the Activity 
sheet ‘Viking longships 2’. These sheets focus on the 
structure of the longship and why it was such an 
impressive vessel. 
The Activity sheet ‘Building a longship’ is a good 
activity for kinaesthetic learners and encourages 
students to imagine a Viking journey by longship.
Finally, the Activity sheet ‘Viking ships versus 
modern technology’ emphasises the differences 
between Viking and modern sea craft.
Extension activity
Vikings ships were made of wood. Ask students to 
consider why this might have been the case. For 
example, wood was easy to harvest and work with, 
and it was also a renewable resource (that is, if 
harvested carefully it would not run out). What would 
have been the advantages of using wood? What 
would have been the disadvantages?

uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.title: The Vikings - Viking beliefs
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.subject: History
