ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
35
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Viking beliefs
Objectives
l	 Understand that beliefs influence behaviour 
and the study of belief systems is an important 
aspect of historical investigation 
l	 Identify the most significant aspects of Norse 
mythology (i.e. the three worlds of the universe, 
the Norse creation myth, Valhalla and the most 
important Norse gods) 
l	 Introduce students to Viking funerary customs
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge required.
Background
The Vikings had a complex and interesting 
mythology. A mythology is a collection of stories 
used to explain the world, the creation and role of 
humans in the natural world, and the relationships 
between humans and gods. This mythology (and the 
beliefs that accompanied it) influenced the way the 
Vikings lived and fought, and underscored a host of 
their social behaviours.
Starter activity
When we study people from the past, it is important 
to think about the things they believed in. Belief 
systems influence laws and can shape the way 
people interact with each other. Use the following 
questions to encourage class discussion regarding 
the way present-day beliefs affect our society: 
l  Why do most people believe it is important to 
obey laws? How does this belief affect behaviour?
l  What do some people believe happens when they 
die? How might these beliefs affect the way they 
live their lives?
l  What are some positive effects of people having 
different belief systems?
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘The Norse 
universe’ before completing the Activity sheet ‘A 
complex mythology’. You might like to search the 
internet for pictorial representations of the Norse 
universe so that students are able to visualise the 
three world levels.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Norse 
mythology’ before completing the Activity sheet 
‘Understanding Norse mythology’. These sheets 
introduce students to the Norse creation myth and a 
handful of important gods.
The Activity sheet ‘Valhalla’ examines Viking beliefs 
about the afterlife and Viking funerary customs. 
Extension activity
A society’s funerary customs are strongly influenced by 
its belief systems. What do the funerary customs of our 
society say about us? Take a poll within the class. How 
many funerals have students attended? How were the 
funerals conducted? For example, was the deceased 
person buried or cremated, and was the funeral a 
religious or secular event? Be aware that some students 
may find it upsetting to talk about funerals they have 
attended, so make sure all discussion is voluntary.

uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.title: The Vikings - Crafty Vikings
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.subject: History
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.description: Vikings and the Medieval World. Teaching Guide.
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.searchText:
ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
41
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Crafty Vikings 
Objectives
l	 Recognise the inventiveness and creativity of 
the Vikings  
l	 Identify the influence of Viking inventions on 
future generations 
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge required. 
Background
Despite their limited resources, the Vikings were 
very crafty people. Not only were they exceptional 
boatbuilders, they also invented lots of things we 
still use today, such as the magnetic compass. The 
Vikings had their own alphabet, called the futhark, 
and their weapons were more advanced than others 
of their time. The harsh conditions experienced by 
the Vikings may well have inspired them to think up 
ways to make their lives just that little bit easier. 
Starter activity
What does the phrase ‘necessity is the mother of 
invention’ mean? Provide some examples of things 
that have been invented in response to specific 
needs. 
Resource and Activity sheets
This unit contains five Activity sheets, the first four of 
which explore different aspects of Viking inventiveness. 
The Activity sheet ‘Ready for battle’ introduces students 
to weapons used by the Vikings. The Activity sheet 
‘Clothing and armour’ describes the clothing and 
armour worn by Viking men and women. The Activity 
sheet ‘Clever Vikings’ introduces students to four Viking 
inventions. The Activity sheet ‘The futhark’ describes 
the Viking alphabet and invites students to create 
messages using the alphabet. 
The final Activity sheet, ‘Viking accomplishments’, 
contains a crossword that includes various aspects 
of Viking inventiveness and culture that have been 
covered in the unit. The answers to the crossword clues 
are: ACROSS: 2 leather; 4 chainmail; 7 comb; 9 futhark; 
10 spear; 12 axes; 13 sword. DOWN: 1 cloth; 3 metal;  
4 compass; 5 loom; 6 cloak; 8 saex; 10 shield; 11 iron;  
14 skis; 15 warp.
Extension activity
As a class, brainstorm a list of recent inventions that we 
live with or use during this modern age. Of these, which 
inventions are likely to stand the test of time and still 
be around in 500 years? Why will they still be relevant 
then? What ensures that an item will not date and will 
continue to be needed over time?

uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.title: The Vikings - Viking conquests
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.subject: History
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/A.description: Vikings and the Medieval World. Teaching Guide.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
47
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Viking conquests 
Objectives
l	 Recognise the links between the Viking raids 
and the Vikings’ expansion throughout Europe 
and beyond
l	 Understand the reasons why the Vikings raided 
villages, cities and monasteries, and why those 
raids were generally successful
l	 Consider the effects of raids on the people 
being raided
l	 Develop some skills at interpreting a primary 
source
Prior knowledge
Students should have basic map-reading skills, 
including an understanding of the location of 
Europe. 
Background
Throughout the three centuries that the Vikings 
dominated Europe, it was violence and the threat 
of violence that made their conquests possible. 
Viking raids were sudden, swift and destructive. 
People were killed or enslaved, items of value were 
stolen and many raided villages were left ablaze. 
The Danegeld evolved as a means of appeasing the 
Vikings and protecting people and property. 
Starter activity
What is a raid? Ask students to look up the word in a 
dictionary and write the definition in their workbooks. 
Invite students to brainstorm reasons why raids 
would have been an effective way of dominating a 
region. Write their responses on the board. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Viking raids’ and 
then complete the Activity sheet ‘Conquered by Vikings’. 
The Resource sheet emphasises the fact that Vikings 
saw raids as battles rather than acts of theft.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Lindisfarne 1’ 
and complete the Activity sheet ‘Lindisfarne 2’ in small 
groups. This Activity sheet may be difficult for some 
students; you may need to help them with interpreting 
the language used in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 
excerpt. 
The final Activity sheet, ‘Danegeld – paying off the 
Vikings’, can be completed by students individually. 
This sheet combines grammatical knowledge with 
an understanding of the Danegeld. The final exercise 
invites students to consider the effect of the Danegeld 
on farmers at the time.
Extension activity
Play the game ‘Viking Quest’ on the BBC History 
website. This game invites students to build a ship, 
cross the seas, loot a monastery and return home to 
claim their prize. The village chieftain then determines 
whether the raid has been a success or not. The 
game lasts approximately 5–7 minutes per go and is 
designed as an educational resource. It can be accessed 
by visiting the BBC website at www.bbc.co.uk/history/
ancient/vikings/launch_gms_viking_quest.shtml 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
53
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Trade and expansion
Objectives
l	 Understand what trade is and why studying it 
is an important part of historical studies
l	 Identify some of the items traded by Vikings 
l	 Identify key trading locations and routes
l	 Introduce students to Erik the Red, a Viking 
committed to the expansion of Viking trade 
Prior knowledge
Students should have some geographical 
knowledge and an understanding of where 
the Vikings came from. They should also know 
the location of key countries in Europe (such as 
England, France and Spain) and Russia. 
Background
Aided by their prowess as sailors and their success 
with raiding, the Vikings were exceptional traders 
who built extensive and complex trade networks. 
Many trade ports and cities were either founded 
or expanded by the Vikings, with the settlement 
of these ports and cities being one of the central 
factors in their dominance. 
Starter activity
Who do we trade with? Think about the various 
cities, states and countries we trade with. Do certain 
goods tend to be associated with a particular 
country? If so, which goods and which countries? Do 
trade relations matter? How well do you think your 
town/city/nation would survive if it didn’t trade with 
other people? Are there certain items you simply 
wouldn’t have were it not for trade?
Resource and Activity sheets
Students should work with a partner to complete 
the Activity sheet ‘Trade matters’. This Activity sheet 
encourages students to consider the role of trade in 
history as well as in their own time. 
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘The Vikings as 
traders’ then complete the Activity sheet ‘Viking trade’. 
These sheets explore the role Viking trade played in 
expanding commodities throughout the world. 
Finally, students can read the Resource sheet ‘Erik the 
Red’ before completing the Activity sheet ‘Erik the Red 
expands Viking trade’. These sheets examine the role of 
Erik the Red in the colonisation of Greenland.
Extension activity
This activity is designed to show students how 
extensive modern trade routes are, and how we tend 
to take them for granted. The students are required to 
complete the first section as homework. 
Each student should select two items of food from 
their pantry at home. They should write down the name 
of each item, as well as the name of the country it came 
from (this information is on the label, but you might 
need to explain this to students first). 
In class, on a large map of the world, write all the 
food items recorded by the students and mark the 
countries that these items came from. 
How wide-ranging is global trade? How does it 
compare to trade during the Viking Age?

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
59
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Did the Vikings  
discover North America? 
Objectives
l	 Understand what is meant by an artefact, a 
fossil and a primary source
l	 Learn about the location and historical 
relevance of L’anse aux Meadows 
l	 Recognise how far from Scandinavia the 
Vikings travelled
Prior knowledge
Students should have some basic map-reading 
skills and be able to identify Scandinavia, Europe 
and North America. 
Background
Christopher Columbus is credited with being the 
first European explorer to discover North America. 
However, as recently as the 1960s a small group of 
archaeologists found proof of Viking settlement in a 
small coastal village in North America. The discovery 
of Viking artefacts at L’anse aux Meadows confirmed 
that the Vikings had discovered at least this small 
part of the North American coastline, many centuries 
ahead of Christopher Columbus. 
Starter activity
How does the stuff that we leave behind give others 
clues as to how we lived? Divide the class into small 
groups. Give each group a sheet of paper with a list 
of items on it. One list may have, for example, a teddy 
bear, a dummy, a bag of nappies, a bag of wool with 
knitting needles, a rocking chair, a pair of spectacles, 
a range of cake tins, a rolling pin, one bed and one 
cot, and a closet full of women’s clothing. Tell each 
group that they have to hypothesise, based on the 
evidence left behind, who lived in the house where 
the items were found, how old they may have been 
and what sex they were. Invite each group to also 
make up a theory as to why the inhabitants of the 
house disappeared. Each group can present their 
findings to the rest of the class. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘Artefacts, fossils 
and primary sources’ before completing the Activity 
sheet ‘Unearthing the past’. These sheets help students 
learn how to distinguish between artefacts and fossils, 
and how to identify primary sources. Students may 
require additional support and explanation in order 
to understand what a fossil is. A good website to visit 
is www.oum.ox.ac.uk/thezone/fossils/intro/form.htm, 
which is hosted by the Oxford University Museum of 
Natural History.
Students can read the Resource sheet ‘The artefacts 
of L’anse aux Meadow’ before completing the Activity 
sheet ‘Artefact detective work’. These sheets encourage 
students to deduce behaviours by using primary 
evidence.
Finally, students can work with a partner to complete 
the Activity sheet ‘The Vikings and North America’. 
Extension activity
What is the Arctic Circle? Working in pairs, students can 
research online (using internet search engines such as 
Firefox or Google) what the Arctic Circle is, where it is 
located, how cold the region is and how icy conditions 
hamper sea travel. Students can then produce an 
information booklet on the Arctic Circle region. The 
information booklet should be produced with a Viking 
reader in mind and should contain basic details as well 
as possible tips on how to survive in this region. 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

The Vikings were a bold people. They were great explorers and excellent sailors.

The Vikings were so legendary that, even today, most people have some idea of who

The Viking Age 
The Vikings ruled much of Europe for centuries. In fact, the years between c. 790 CE and  
c. 1066 CE became known as the Viking Age.
Scandinavia
The Vikings came from Scandinavia. Scandinavia is a region in northern Europe that 
is centred on the Scandinavian Peninsula. A peninsula is a piece of land that is mainly 
surrounded by water. The Scandinavian Peninsula is the largest peninsula in Europe.
Today, Scandinavia is made up of three countries:
●	 Denmark       
●	 Norway       
● Sweden.
Resource sheet – Who were the Vikings?
This map shows the Scandinavian Peninsula and the 
three countries that make up Scandinavia.
The people who lived in Scandinavia from c. 790 CE were exceptional boatbuilders 
and sailors, so they were able to raid and trade throughout the region. These people 
came to be known as Vikings. Before the Viking Age, many other peoples had lived in 
Scandinavia, such as the Goths, the Vandals, the Cimbri and the Angles.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
12
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Mountains, plains and lots of water 
Today, Scandinavia is made up of three countries called Norway, Denmark and Sweden. 
Each of these countries has its own unique natural features, but there are some things 
they all have in common. They are all cold countries, they all have access to waterways 
such as rivers and seas, and they all have hundreds of islands and jagged coastlines. A 
jagged coastline has a lot of bays and inlets, which makes it easy to travel short or long 
distances by boat because there are many places to land.
●
●Norway has high plateaus and wide ranges of tall mountains. The lowland in the 
valleys and on the plains is very fertile and good for growing crops. Norway’s 
coastline has lots of fjords. A fjord is a long, narrow inlet with high cliffs on either 
side. Fjords are formed by glaciers that have long since disappeared into the sea. 
●
●Denmark has a long, rugged coastline. Most of the land is quite low and flat. There 
are lots of rivers and inland seas, and much of the land inside the coast is below sea 
level. There are also many marshes (land covered in grasses and reeds that often 
floods) and moors (very wet, open land that is exposed to sea winds).
●
●Sweden is ten times larger than Denmark but doesn’t have as much coastline. It has 
areas of low rolling plains, as well as mountains to the west. The soil is usually sandy 
and rocky, although there are small areas of fertile soil. Sweden has lots of lakes and 
waterfalls. 
The Vikings had a hard time growing food because of the weather and the landscape, 
as well as the lack of fertile soil. This was one of the main reasons the Vikings travelled 
beyond Scandinavia.

18
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Farming and raiding
Viking farmers 
My name is Magnus. I am a Viking farmer.
Most Vikings are farmers. People think of us only as fearsome pirates, but 
there is more to us than that. When we aren’t sailing to new lands, we are 
tending our small farms and looking after our families.
I grow crops such as onions, leeks, peas, beans and cabbages. My friend, 
Ivar, grows cereals such as barley, oats and rye.
Farming is difficult work. The soil is hard and poor. It takes a lot of effort 
to break it up, so we use oxen to help us plough the fields. We cannot sow 
crops through the winter because of the snow, so we only have a few 
seasons a year in which to grow food.
Viking farms have animals, but the animals must be tough to withstand 
the cold. We have some cattle and sheep. The manure from the animals 
is good for the soil. The sheep survive the cold well, and they give us milk 
as well as meat. Ivar also has pigs. Sometimes the cold is so harsh that the 
animals get sick. We do not have the time or food to care for sick animals, 
so if an animal is injured or starving we kill it and eat it straightaway. 
My son’s favourite food is fish. He is a great fisherman. 
He has had lots of practice because we live so close 
to the sea. He also gathers seaweed for his mother, 
although he hates eating it. My son is a good boy. 
He will grow up to be an honourable man.

Away on a Viking raid
Resource sheet – Farming and raiding
My name is Ingrid. My husband Rolf and I have five children. Rolf is often away 
for months at a time on raids. A raid is a very fast, surprise attack. While he 
is gone, I take care of all the household chores, as well as looking after the 
animals on the farm.
Our Viking men are famous for their raids. People fear being attacked by them 
because the attacks usually come as a surprise, and are swift and brutal.
Rolf is a strong man. He is one of the oarsmen in the longship the men take on 
their raids. He is a fearsome warrior. I find it hard to imagine him terrorising 
people; at home he is so gentle.
When we were first married, I asked Rolf not to leave me to go on raids. He 
explained that the raids are important. We do not have much land suitable for 
growing crops or grazing. As our villages grow, we need to find other places 
to farm and raise our families. The raids also help improve our trading options. 
By taking over key cities, we are able to use new trade routes.
Rolf told me that the longships they sail are fast and agile (able to move 
quickly and easily). They can be sailed up rivers and brought in 
close to towns and villages. He said the raids are carefully 
planned and the weapons he uses are stronger than those 
used by his enemies.
My husband is very proud of his skill as a sailor and 
warrior. Our eldest son sees the glory that his father 
receives and wants to follow in his father’s footsteps.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
21
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012

went on were still dangerous missions.

case for and the case against. An example argument has been done for you.

The case against raiding

monasteries to get the food we need 
in order to survive the long, cold winter 
months.
Raiding is dangerous and what little food

will probably not last the rough journey 
home.

Viking hierarchy
There were three classes of people in Viking society: jarls, karls and thralls.
Class

Interesting fact
Jarls
Jarls were wealthy 
nobles who owned large 
properties, ships and 
treasures.
The most important jarl 
was a king. Each region 
had a king.
Jarls lived in large, 
fancy halls. Their lives 
were comfortable 
compared with those 
of the other classes. 
Jarls were only as 
powerful as the people 
who supported them. 
A good jarl knew he 
had to take care of his 
followers so that he 
could remain in power. 
Karls
Karls were landowners, 
farmers and other 
freemen, such as 
carpenters and 
blacksmiths. 
Karl families tended to 
live close to other karls. 
They usually lived in 
longhouses and used 
other buildings (such 
as barns) as well. 
If a karl worked hard 
and became wealthy 
and famous enough, 
he could become a jarl.
Thralls
Thralls were slaves and 
bondsmen.
Slaves were used to 
help run farms, go 
on raids and row the 
Viking boats. They 
lived hard lives and 
had few rights. If they 
had a generous jarl 
and were able to save, 
they could buy their 
freedom. 
If a Viking could not 
pay his debt, he would 
be forced to become a 
bondsman. This meant 
he would have to work 
for someone else until 
he had cleared what he 
owed.
Some people – such as beggars and outlaws – did not belong to any of these classes. 
Beggars could not afford to own land and so they had no legal rights. They couldn’t 
pass on anything they owned to their children when they died, and they weren’t 
allowed to marry.

The role of Viking women
+	 1	 Read the passage below, then match the underlined words in the passage with

Viking society was patriarchal. Men made the laws, spoke at important meetings 
called ‘things’ and could be elected kings. Women weren’t allowed to do any of these 
things. They did, however, have more rights than most women living in other parts of 
Europe at the time. 
Viking girls usually got married in their early teens. Before a girl married, her father 
had authority over her. After she was married, her husband had authority over her. 
Viking women were in charge of looking after their homes and their families. They 
were responsible for all the household chores. They also had to run the family farm or 
estate when their husbands were away. Wealthy Viking women had slaves to help them, 
but most Vikings were not wealthy. Viking women did not go on raids or sail away on 
trading trips.
Viking women were expected to behave with honour, just like Viking men. They were 
proud, generous and strong-willed. Viking men were expected to treat their women with 
respect.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
28
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Things – Viking meetings
The Vikings used a special system of law-making meetings, called ‘things’. There were 
local things and regional things. In Iceland, there was also a national thing called the 
Althing. At a thing, free Viking men would discuss laws and settle arguments. 
●
●First, at a local thing, the karls (freemen) of each region would select a chieftain that 
they wanted to support. The chieftain, called a godi, represented his people at regional 
things. He had to take as many supporters as possible to a thing, just in case a fight  
broke out. Also, the more supporters he had, the more powerful he would be. Chieftains 
knew they had to look after their followers if they wanted to keep their support. 
●
●All the chieftains from all the regions would attend the national things. Things could 
last several days. The Althing – held annually in summer – would last a couple of 
weeks. There would be much feasting and drinking during this time.
●
●Viking laws were not written down like our laws today. Instead, a Viking lawman 
would memorise the laws and recite them at the beginning of each thing. 
●
●Vikings would also elect their regional king at the regional thing. Viking kings had 
to be honourable, generous and brave fighters, and they had to be able to inspire 
other warriors.
Similar or different?
+	 1	 Below are some features of our modern-day system of government. Are these 
features similar or different to a Viking thing? Tick the correct box.
Similar to a 
Viking thing
Different to a 
Viking thing
In our modern governments, all laws must be 
written down.
In our modern governments, elected officials 
need to keep their followers happy otherwise 
the officials can be voted out.
In our modern governments, women can be 
elected to represent the people.
In our modern governments, we do not 
expect our leaders to be good warriors.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
30
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
The Vikings and their boats 
The Vikings were excellent boatbuilders and sailors. They built three main types of boats:
●
●longships (also known as dragon-ships)
●
●merchant ships 
●
●small boats.
The most famous Viking sea craft was the longship. Longships were narrow and about as 
long as a basketball court. This made it easy for them to move quickly over the water. The hull 
(main body of the ship) was also very shallow, so it could sail in water only one metre deep 
or right up onto a beach. Another great thing about longships was that the bow (front of 
the ship) and stern (back of the ship) were identical. This meant that longships could change 
direction very quickly. Longships were used mainly to transport troops during times of war. 
The Vikings also built merchant ships to transport goods between cities and countries. 
There were large and small merchant ships. Large merchant ships were used to carry heavy  
loads. They weren’t as long as longships, but they were very wide. The hulls of the large mer­chant 
ships were deep so that they could carry a lot of goods, and these ships sailed the open

The most common type of Viking watercraft were small boats. These boats were used for

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
31
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Viking longships 1
The Vikings worked hard to make their longships the fastest and most agile ships of their 
day. They did this in three ways:
●
●They built their boats using wood. Wood is a light material that floats well, is easy 
to work with and moves quickly over water. It is also a material that was easy to 
find in Scandinavia. 
●
●They attached a large square sail to a central mast. The sail was enormous, so it was 
good at catching a lot of wind. It was made of linen or wool and then covered in 
animal fat to make it waterproof. Ropes made of hemp or horsehair held the sail in 
place. The sail was designed so that it could be turned easily to catch the wind from 
any direction. 
●
●They made the longships large enough so that they could fit several oarsmen 
along each side. That way, when the wind died down and they couldn’t use the sail, 
they would still have enough manpower to row the ship.
The Vikings tried to make their longships look as scary as possible. They often dyed 
their large sails red, like blood, to frighten their enemies. They carved large dragon-like 
heads and added these to the prows of their longships.  The Vikings believed that these 
would scare the spirits that lived in the towns and villages they raided. They removed 
the prow heads when they were sailing home, so that their families would not be 
frightened.

36
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
The Norse universe
Viking mythology is usually called Norse mythology. ‘Norse’ simply means that it came 
from Scandinavia during the Viking era.
Norse mythology was full of courage, hardship and larger-than-life characters. It 
contained magic, as well as elves, giants and dwarfs. Norse mythology was strongly based 
on the natural environment. Trees, the sky, forests and snow all featured in its stories.  
According to Norse mythology, there were three worlds that made up the universe:
●
●Asgard
●
●Midgard
●
●Niflheim.
The first world, Asgard, was where the gods of war and the gods of the sky lived. 
Asgard was full of wondrous halls and palaces made of silver and gold. The most brilliant 
of these halls was Valhalla. Elves and the Vanir (fertility gods who could see into the 
future) also lived here. 
The second world was Midgard (which means the Middle World). Human beings lived 
in Midgard. Midgard was a fortress built by the gods and given to the Vikings to help 
protect them from the giants. Giants, dark elves and dwarfs lived on the same level as 
human beings, but in separate lands. 
Between Asgard and Midgard was a huge 
and beautiful rainbow bridge called Bifrost. 
Anyone could use the bridge to travel between 
worlds but the journey was always very 
dangerous, even for the gods.
Finally, there was an underworld called 
Niflheim (which means land of the mists). 
Niflheim was also known as Hel, named after  
the goddess of the dead who ruled there.  
It was an icy, cold place and one that was  
feared by the Vikings.

Norse mythology
According to Norse mythology, there once lived a frightful giant made of frost, called 
Ymir. One day, the god Odin set out with his two brothers, Vili and Ve, to kill Ymir. They 
succeeded. They then made the Earth with Ymir’s body and the sky with Ymir’s skull. The 
seas and rivers were created from Ymir’s blood. Odin and his brothers then created the 
first human beings. The first man was created from an ash tree, and the first woman was 
created from an elm tree. 
Odin lived with other gods in Asgard. Asgard was the land of the Aesir (warrior gods) 
and the Vanir (sky gods). Odin was the father and ruler of all the gods, and he ruled over 
all human beings and other living creatures. Odin was also the god of war, wisdom, poetry 
and magic. He could create battles on Earth by throwing down his spear. He also liked to 
choose the winner of any war between humans. The Vikings did all they could to keep 
Odin happy so that he would favour them in battles.

Clothing and armour 
The Vikings wore simple, warm clothes that they made from wool, flax and linen. Men 
wore plain pants with a tunic over the top. Women wore long dresses. Both wore long 
thick cloaks made of felted wool to protect them during cold days. 
+	 1   What sort of clothes do people wear now? What are they made of?
_________________________________________________________________________
_________________________________________________________________________
_________________________________________________________________________
Vikings wore shoes made from leather, and their belts were made of leather or rope. They 
liked to decorate their clothes and made intricate (complicated and detailed) braid trims 
for important pieces of clothing. Pins were used to fasten clothes and cloaks. The pins 
were made of bone or metal and sometimes even gold.
2   What are your shoes made of? Did you make them yourself? 
_________________________________________________________________________
_________________________________________________________________________
In battle, men wore chainmail over their tunics to protect them from sword blows. 
The chainmail was made of small metal rings bound together. It covered a man’s torso 
as well as his upper arms and legs. Chainmail was expensive and heavy to wear, so not 
everyone wore it. Many men chose instead to wear body armour made of leather and 
quilted cloth. Helmets were made of iron, with a nose plate to 
protect the nose and a guard to protect the eyes.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
48
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Viking raids
For centuries, the Vikings sailed their way throughout much of Europe, attacking villages 
as they went. One of the first and most famous Viking raids took place at the monastery 
at Lindisfarne, in northern England. A monastery is a place where a community of monks 
or nuns lives. Vikings attacked monasteries because they were poorly defended and those 
who lived there had no weapons. Monasteries also often held lots of valuable things, such 
as gold, food, animals and jewels. 
During raids, the Vikings would burn buildings, kill people, take women and children 
as slaves, and steal any riches they found. The Vikings did not see raiding as stealing. They 
were very proud and honourable people. They believed that stealing was a terrible act 
and if you stole something you would have a horrible afterlife. Instead, they saw raids as 
honourable battles in which the victor (the winning side) was allowed to keep the spoils 
of war (all the valuable items that they took from the losing side). 
Viking raids were very successful for a few reasons. Firstly, the Vikings could sneak up 
quietly in their boats and take villages and monasteries by surprise. Secondly, raids were 
known to be fierce and bloody, so people often ran away or surrendered. The Vikings 
then moved on to the next place just as quickly as they had arrived.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
50
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Lindisfarne 1
In 793 CE, Vikings attacked a monastery at Lindisfarne. Lindisfarne is a small island off the 
north-eastern coast of England. The monastery contained many religious relics (historical 
objects). It was also an important centre of learning. 
The raid was swift and brutal. Many monks were killed, and some were taken as slaves. 
The monastery was burned and valuable items were stolen. After the raid, the remaining 
monks fled Lindisfarne with whatever relics they had managed to save.
The following account of the Viking raid at Lindisfarne was recorded in the Anglo-Saxon 
Chronicle. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is a collection of historical records written in England 
between the 9th and 12th centuries. It is an example of a primary historical source, 
which means that it was created during the historical period that is being studied.
Resource sheet – Viking conquests
This year came dreadful fore-warnings over the 
land of the Northumbrians, terrifying the people 
most woefully: these were immense sheets of 
light rushing through the air, and whirlwinds, and 
fiery dragons flying across the firmament. These 
tremendous tokens were soon followed by a great 
famine: and not long after, on the sixth day before 
the ides of January in the same year, the harrowing 
inroads of heathen men made lamentable havoc 
in the church of God in Holy-island [Lindisfarne], 
by rapine and slaughter.

Achieve!
Danegeld – paying off the Vikings
A proper noun refers to the name of a person, place, group, event or important object. 
Examples of proper nouns are ‘England’ and ‘Ingrid’. Proper nouns start with a capital 
letter. A common noun is the name given to a type of person, place or thing. Examples of 
common nouns are ‘chair’, ‘boat’ and ‘men’. 
+	
1   Identify whether the underlined words below are common nouns or proper 
nouns by circling the correct option. 
Viking raids were organised and brutal. Few cities survived a Viking raid and 
most people – including rulers (common noun / proper noun) – were scared 
of being attacked and killed. 
In 810 CE, more than 200 Viking ships (common noun / proper noun) 
attacked a place called Frisia (common noun / proper noun). The Vikings 
demanded a bounty (a lot of money) in return for not destroying the area. 
The people of Frisia gave them 45 kilograms of silver (common noun / 
proper noun). This payment came to be known as Danegeld (common 
noun / proper noun), which means ‘Danish gold’. Over time, the Danegeld 
became a way of paying off the Vikings so that they wouldn’t attack. To raise 
the money (common noun / proper noun) needed to pay the Vikings, kings 
(common noun / proper noun) charged their people a Danegeld tax. 
The Danegeld was commonly used as a way of avoiding Viking attacks for 
300 years. During that time (common noun / proper noun), many tonnes of 
silver were given to the Vikings. In return, the Vikings would agree to settle 
in an area (common noun / proper noun) and rule it fairly without violence. 
Sometimes the Vikings would take the silver and return to Scandinavia 
(common noun / proper noun). 
2	 Imagine you were a farmer living in England. How would you have felt about having to 
pay the Danegeld tax? Write your answer in your workbook.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
54
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Trade matters
Trade refers to the buying and selling of goods and services between people. Trade can 
happen within a village, or it can take place between different countries. 
Throughout history, people have exchanged goods. Historians know, for example, that 
even in the Stone Age humans in different areas exchanged one type of rock (flint) for 
another (obsidian). As civilisations grew and people began to travel further, they traded 
with people from other cities and then other countries. 
Archaeologists and historians like to study the trading habits of people who lived long 
ago. It gives them information about a lot of things, such as:
●
●what items were considered valuable enough to trade with
●
●which peoples and countries traded with each other
●
●where trading took place (for example, in a market or in a port)
●
●how items that came from one culture ended up somewhere completely different
●
●what the most common land and sea trade routes were.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
55
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
The Vikings as traders
The Vikings were great traders. Their skills as sailors made it possible for them to travel 
between countries, and their large boats helped them carry goods from one place to another. 
As the Vikings travelled further, to other countries throughout Europe and towards 
Asia, they traded with different peoples. They traded the furs they hunted as well as wood, 
wool, leather, honey and other items for silver, silk, jewellery, weapons and spices. 
The Vikings also bought and sold slaves. During Viking raids, local people were taken by 
the Vikings and enslaved. These slaves were then taken to Viking settlements to work or 
taken to other cities to be traded. Slave trading was common throughout most parts of 
Europe during the Viking Age.
Many cities and ports in Europe were created or expanded by the Vikings through 
trade. For example, the Vikings founded Dublin in Ireland and Birka in Sweden. They also 
traded with people as far east as Russia. 
The Vikings created a complex network of trade routes over land and sea. These 
routes covered Scandinavia, most of Europe, the northern part of the Atlantic Ocean and 
the Mediterranean area. Historians know where the Vikings traded because they have 
found Viking artefacts in these areas.

Erik the Red
Resource sheet – Trade and expansion
My name is Erik the Red. I was born in Norway in 950 CE. My full name is  
Erik Thorvaldsson. People call me ‘Red’ because I have red hair.
I moved from Norway to Iceland with my parents. When I was 32 years 
old, I killed several people. I was then exiled (barred) from Iceland for 
three years.
I decided to spend that time sailing and exploring other lands. I discovered a 
place I called Greenland. No Vikings or other Europeans lived there. I liked the 
idea of living away from all the people I had fought with back in Iceland.
Once my three-year exile was finished, I sailed back to Iceland. I told people 
how wonderful Greenland was. I figured the name ‘Greenland’ would make 
it sound like a nice place to live, and I was right. Lots of people decided to 
come back with me. In 986 CE we left Iceland and sailed to Greenland.
We started up two colonies in Greenland. Both were on the south-west 
coast, as the land there was better for farming. In summer, men from both 
colonies would travel north to hunt seals and whales for their meat, and 
walruses for their tusks. Life was tough. It was very cold and sea ice made 
sailing difficult. We also fought from time to time with the 
native Inuits.
My son, Leif Eriksson, eventually left Greenland and 
explored Vinland (North America). I was to have gone with 
him, but I changed my mind. I never saw my son again.

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
60
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Artefacts, fossils and  
primary sources
An artefact is an object that was made by people long ago. Artefacts could be something 
natural that humans reshaped (such as a flint knife) or they could be items that involved 
a lot of work (such as a decorated bowl). Artefacts usually lie forgotten and buried for 
years – sometimes hundreds or thousands of years – before being rediscovered by 
archaeologists. 
Archaeologists study the past. They visit areas where people lived and excavate these 
sites looking for artefacts. They use special tools to scrape and brush away soil. They work 
very slowly and carefully to uncover artefacts without breaking them. 
Artefacts are called primary sources because they come from the actual historical 
period that is being studied. Historians can use primary sources to work out what life was 
like during a specific time in history. 
Not all artefacts survive. Some artefacts – such as clothes made of wool – decay 
over time or decay underground. Others might be washed away in storms or taken by 
explorers. 
A fossil is a very different thing from an artefact. An artefact is something that was 
made by people. A fossil, on the other hand, is the remains or the impression of something 
that was once alive long ago. There are two main types of fossils – animal fossils and plant 
fossils. 
Resource sheet – Did the Vikings  
discover North America?
      Artefacts, such as handmade weapons,  
    tell us about life long ago.

61
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Unearthing the past

ACHIEVE!   History – The ancient to the modern world: The Vikings 1
62
© Siboney Duff and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
The artefacts of L’anse aux Meadow
The Vikings told long elaborate tales, called sagas. These sagas were passed on orally 
from one generation to the next. Then, between the 12th and 14th centuries, the 
sagas were written down. The sagas told of Viking kings, battles and great journeys. For  
a long time, historians didn’t know whether any part of the sagas was real or if it was  
all make-believe. 
One of the sagas told the story of Leif Eriksson and his discovery of a place called 
Vinland. Some historians thought that Vinland may be in North America – but they had 
no proof. Then in the 1960s, a group of archaeologists discovered the remains of a Viking 
village in a place called L’anse aux Meadows, on the island of Newfoundland, off the 
eastern coast of Canada. 
Archaeologists uncovered many things at L’anse aux Meadows. Among them were:
●
●the foundations of eight Viking buildings
●
●the remains of a fireplace
●
●a bronze pin
●
●a stone oil lamp
●
●a spindle whorl (for spinning wool) made of stone
●
●some needles made of bone
●
●a small pair of scissors.

Achieve!   history – The ancient world: china 1
5
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Introducing ancient China
Prior knowledge
Students should have some basic map-reading skills 
and be able to identify Australia in an atlas.
Background
Ancient China covers a long period of history, 
spanning several dynasties. China differed greatly 
from one dynasty to another. This unit aims to clarify 
the historical time periods of ancient China, as well 
as introducing important features, such as emperors 
and dynasties. This unit also introduces the terms BC/
AD and BCE/CE, timelines and primary and secondary 
sources, as students will need to be familiar with these 
terms when undertaking further historical study.
Starter activity
Hold a class brainstorm to find out what students 
know about ancient China. Encourage students to 
come up with ideas without worrying about whether 
they are right or wrong. You may wish to give each 
student a whiteboard marker so they can write their 
idea on the board, or you may ask them to come 
up with ideas in small groups and then share them 
with the class. After you have talked through their 
responses, ask the students where they got their ideas 
from. Prompt them to discuss the internet, movies, 
books, cartoons and anything else they may have 
gathered information from. Ask them to be specific 
about which sources they have found the most  
useful and why.
Resource and Activity sheets
As a class, read through the Activity sheet, ‘Ancient 
China’. Ask the students to identify any words that 
they do not understand and provide definitions for 
students to write in their workbooks. Working out the 
distance from China to Australia could be done as a 
class. The aim of this work sheet is to give students 
a geographic understanding of China, as well as an 
introduction to ancient China. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Ruling families’, consolidates the 
information about emperors and dynasties from the 
‘Ancient China’ Resource sheet, as well as explaining 
the variety of spellings used when Chinese names 
are written in English. The areas of interest should be 
shared in class to find common ground. This could also 
help with directing class topics or external research 
projects. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Recording time’, should be read 
before completing the Activity sheet, ‘Timeline’,  
to ensure that students understand the difference 
between BC/AD and BCE/CE. This is very important when 
studying ancient China, as dates may refer to BC/BCE 
events or AD/CE events.
The Activity sheet, ‘Primary and secondary sources’, 
explains the difference between these two sources of 
information, as well as demonstrating why both are 
important.
Extension ideas
• Students could compare the size of China to their 
own country, then list reasons why the size might 
have made it difficult for the emperors to maintain 
control. 
• The ancient Chinese mostly travelled over land on 
foot or by camel, horseback or carriage and over 
water on ships and boats. Students could measure 
the distance from one end of China to the other and 
work out which forms of transport they would use. 
Students could also consider how the forms  
of transport might be different if they were rich  
or poor.
• Students could measure how long it takes them to 
walk one kilometre and then work out how long it 
would take them to walk to different locations in 
China: from one city to another and from one end  
to another.
Objectives
• Identify important historical features of ancient 
China
• Recognise the difference between primary and 
secondary sources
• Identify recognised historical periods for 
ancient China

Achieve!   history – The ancient world: china 1
11
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Geography of ancient China
Prior knowledge
Students should have some basic map-reading skills 
and be able to locate China on a map. 
Background
The geography of China shaped some Chinese 
attitudes towards the outside world. It is a large 
country, bordered by a sea on one side and a large 
mountain range on the other. The ancient Chinese 
belief that foreigners were barbarians developed 
largely because they had so little contact with other 
countries and cultures. In the early years of civilisation, 
China was made up of many small kingdoms. Each 
one was valuable in some way: one area might have 
iron ore deposits, another access to a river, another 
good farmland. It was difficult to travel and trade with 
other civilisations. Instead, the kingdoms would trade 
with each other.
The lack of available fuel for fires in ancient China 
meant that food needed to be cooked quickly. This led 
to a tendency to cut food into small pieces and cook 
it in a wok, which in turn influenced Chinese utensils – 
the pieces of food were so small, they could be eaten 
with just chopsticks.
Starter activity
Discuss the importance of climate. What is the 
weather like in Australia? What about in the students’ 
local area?  
How does this affect the things they can do? Think 
about clothing, heating, food and activities. Compare 
this to other countries that students are familiar with. 
How would their behaviour change if they lived in 
another place with a very different climate?
Resource and Activity sheets
As a class, read through the ‘Map skills’ Activity sheet 
and discuss why students need to include BOLTSS in 
any map that they produce. This could lead to a small 
extension activity for the class where they map their 
classroom as a group.
The ‘Land and climate’ Resource sheet introduces 
the different types of areas – tropical, desert and 
mountainous – and their different features.  
Students then use this information to complete the 
Activity sheet, ‘Physical features’. These work sheets 
develop an important geographical understanding 
of ancient China. Identifying the different areas 
encourages students to consider the relationship 
between different locations and different lifestyles.
Students can read the Resource sheet, ‘Growing food’, 
and then use this information to complete the Activity 
sheet, ‘Water: source of life’. 
Extension ideas
• Students could develop their own simple map of 
their home or a made-up island using BOLTSS.
• Students could create a list of the ways they use 
water, including any machines that they use. They 
could then compare this information to the ways 
the ancient Chinese would have used water.
• Students could identify ways to save or reuse water 
today. Why is it important to save water?
• Students could research the monsoon season or 
flooding in the Yellow River to find out how this has 
affected people living in the area.
• Students could create a poster showing the features 
of either desert, tropical or mountainous regions.
Objectives
• To use basic mapping skills (including BOLTSS) 
and to gain an understanding of the features 
landforms of ancient China
• To identify the importance of rivers and 
irrigation to the ancient Chinese civilisation
• For students to compare their lives to those of 
the Chinese people living in ancient China

Achieve!   history – The ancient world: china 1
17
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Social structure
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with the location of 
ancient China and the period in which it existed.
Background
Honour was a very important aspect of ancient 
Chinese society. The social hierarchy was not based 
on the amount of money that people earned, as it is in 
some other societies, but on how groups were seen by 
others in their community. 
The Chou/Zhou period featured a social system similar 
to the medieval feudal system, which comprised 
three tiers of people. The emperor was at the top, 
mandarins, warlords and landowners were in the 
middle and peasants were at the bottom. The groups 
were connected and relied on each other to survive. 
The emperor gave land and military protection 
to the mandarins, warlords and landowners, and 
expected military and government service in return. 
The mandarins, warlords and landowners defended 
the emperor and peasants, and got services from 
the peasants in return. The peasants were protected 
by the upper classes and provided services such as 
servants and food production in return. Every group 
had to give something in order to get something.
Starter activity
Encourage students to think about the way the animal 
kingdom is structured. Ask them which animals they 
would place on top and which would be put on the 
bottom. In small groups, using butcher’s paper, have 
students try to organise the animal kingdom from 
highest to lowest. Ask students to share their ideas as 
a group, giving reasons for their decisions. Why did 
they place certain animals higher or lower? Is it to do 
with power or size or a food chain? Introduce the idea 
of ancient Chinese society and how it was ordered. 
Why were some groups at the top and why were some 
at the bottom? 
Resource and Activity sheets
Introduce the Resource sheet, ‘Social structure 
in ancient China’, then have students answer the 
questions on the Activity sheet, ‘Makers and sellers’. 
These work sheets introduce the hierarchy of ancient 
Chinese society. It may be helpful to discuss social 
hierarchies in general, and why they exist.
In the ‘Farmers’ Activity sheet, students fill in key words 
to complete a passage exploring the role of farmers 
and their place within society. The Activity sheet, 
‘Scholars and officials’, looks at these two positions, 
and encourages students to relate the information 
to their own lives, suggesting equivalent roles in 
present-day society. The final Activity sheet, ‘Emperors’, 
presents a series of cloze activities outlining the life 
of an emperor. Some students may need to refer 
to a dictionary when completing this work sheet. 
Encourage students to see dictionaries as a useful 
source of information if words are unclear.
Extension ideas
• Students could compare one social group in ancient 
China with a modern social group, identifying 
similarities and differences.
• Have students create a glossary of any unfamiliar 
words, then use these to create sentences 
explaining the social structure in ancient China.
• Students could make their own diagram showing 
the hierarchy in ancient Chinese society. Encourage 
them to clearly represent the highest group and the 
lowest group using symbols such as a crown for  
the emperor.
• Students could research craftspeople in ancient 
China and make a list of the kind of objects that 
they made. The following website may be of 
assistance: http://www.ancientchina.co.uk/crafts/
home_set.html
Objectives
• To develop an understanding of the hierarchy 
of social groups in ancient China
• To compare and contrast different social 
groups in ancient China
• To gain an understanding of some of the 
occupations at the time
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

Achieve!   history – The ancient world: china 1
23
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Women
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with the location of 
ancient China and the period in which it existed.
Background
The lives of women in ancient China were often very 
restricted. Society had many expectations of what 
they could and couldn’t do. Most women, as the 
newest and lowest member of their husband’s family, 
had no power. Sometimes, though, if a woman lived 
long enough, she was able to gain some power over 
her daughter-in-law, if she had one, or as the eldest 
member of the family. In families, the eldest member 
was well respected, and was usually considered to be 
the ‘head of the family’, even if she was a woman.  
Even the emperor had to listen to the wishes of his 
older female relatives. 
Starter activity
Ask students to create a mind map showing what they 
believe women’s lives would have been like in ancient 
China. Have them share their findings with the class. 
Resource and Activity sheets
‘Women’s lives’ is a Resource sheet intended to clarify 
the general position of women in ancient China. This 
is supported by the Activity sheet, ‘Now and then’, in 
which students match up definitions and answer some 
true/false questions before comparing the treatment 
of women in ancient China to the present day. If you 
require further information about Confucius, who is 
mentioned briefly in this section, please refer to Unit 8.
The Activity sheet, ‘Girls’ lives’, presents information 
about the treatment of girls in ancient China. When 
reading through this work sheet, encourage students 
to compare this to their own lives.
The ‘Ban Zhao’ Activity sheet may be best done as  
a class task. Students need to use important historio-
graphical skills to analyse different interpretations. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Marriage and divorce’, students 
use synonyms to complete a cloze activity describing 
marriage and divorce in ancient China.
Extension ideas
• Students could research the lives of women in 
ancient Greece and Rome. Compare these to the 
lives of women in ancient China. 
• Each student could write a diary entry explaining 
how they think foot binding would feel, 
remembering that the toes get broken and pushed 
underneath.
• Have each student write a short letter to a woman 
who they find inspirational. This could be a relative, 
a friend or someone famous.
• In pairs, students could list the positives and 
negatives of being a female in ancient China.
Objectives
• To learn about the treatment of women in 
ancient China
• To explore the life of a famous woman who 
lived in ancient China
• To compare and contrast the lives of women in 
the past to now
• To understand the strong importance of the 
family as a unit in China

29
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Everyday life
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with the social structure of 
ancient China.
Background
Everyday life for the ancient Chinese was very 
different to life in Australia today. Although we still 
write, play sports, wear clothes and take medicine, 
in the past these things were done in different ways. 
When playing sports in the past, the focus was not 
on competition but rather on showing your good 
character. It was more important to be a ‘good sport’ 
and behave properly, even when losing, than it was to 
be a physically strong. 
Starter activity
Ask students to draw a picture of the kinds of clothes 
they usually wear. Compare outfits as a class, then 
encourage students to discuss the reasons for their 
chosen outfits. Talk about colours and fashions for boys 
and girls. Are there any differences? Would rich and 
poor people wear different clothes? How might they 
differ? Expand the discussion to consider the clothes 
worn in ancient China and the reasons for these.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet ‘Clothing’ gives students an 
understanding of the clothes worn in ancient China. 
Students draw appropriate clothing onto two 
illustrations to demonstrate their understanding. It 
might be helpful to bring in some pictures of ancient 
Chinese dress for students to refer to. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Medicine’, explores the differences 
between medicine in the past and today. The Resource 
sheet, ‘Writing’, introduces students to Chinese 
writing, and presents a table of pictograms that can 
be used when completing the Activity sheet, ‘Strange 
characters’. The Activity sheet, ‘Sport and recreation’, 
allows students to compare their own experiences 
of sport and recreation to those enjoyed in ancient 
China.
Extension ideas
• Students could draw clothing for all the different 
social groups in ancient China. Encourage them to 
conduct research to ensure that their chosen outfits 
are accurate.
• Have students write a poem or short story about 
living in ancient China. 
• Students could design new clothes for the Emperor 
(encourage them to think about what an emperor 
would wear and why). 
Objectives
• To develop an understanding of everyday life 
in ancient China
• To understand how writing has developed  
over time
• To develop an understanding of the  
similarities and differences between ancient 
and modern life

Achieve!   history – The ancient world: china 1
35
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Law and order
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with the social structure of 
ancient China.
Background
In ancient China it was rare for people to be 
imprisoned for many years, as criminals are today.  
This was because the cost of feeding the criminals was 
so high. However, some people were sentenced to do 
hard labour, as a kind of slavery, on the royal barges, 
in the army or in the mines. Most punishments in 
ancient China tended to involve some kind of physical 
punishment, as a reminder of what would happen to 
people who broke the law. This might mean being 
mutilated, branded or even killed.
Starter activity
Ask the class to come up with 5–10 modern laws. 
Discuss the aim of each law. Is it to punish people?  
To protect the community? Ask the students to rank 
the laws in order of their importance.
Resource and Activity sheets
Students should read the first Resource sheet, ‘Honour 
and crimes’, before completing the Activity sheet, 
‘Honour and dishonour’. These work sheets identify 
the importance of honour and family to the creation of 
laws. Discuss as a class why honour and family were so 
important in ancient China. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Punishments’, introduces the 
forms of punishment commonly used in ancient 
China. The Activity sheet, ‘How were they punished?’, 
presents different types of crimes and asks students 
to determine appropriate punishments, according to 
ancient Chinese law. Discuss how fair or unfair these 
punishments were, particularly where the crimes 
seemed particularly minor. Some of the punishments 
were deliberately harsh in order to keep people from 
reoffending. This may be an uncomfortable topic 
for some students, and some terms may need to be 
explained in class.
The final Activity sheet, ‘Modern law and order’, invites 
students to compare and contrast the laws that we 
have today with those used in ancient China. 
Extension ideas
• Encourage students to imagine that they are stuck 
on a desert island with only the people from their 
class. What laws would they make, and how would 
they punish people who broke those laws? 
• Students could write a diary entry account of a 
witness who saw someone being punished. The 
diary entry should explain how this made the 
person feel.
• Students could list punishments used in ancient 
China and suggest explanations for why each  
was used.
Objectives
• To identify crimes in ancient China and the 
punishments for breaking the law
• To recognise the importance of honour in 
ancient Chinese culture
• To compare and contrast the treatment of 
criminals in modern and ancient societies
• To explore the role of the family in the 
development of laws

Achieve!   history – The ancient world: china 1
41
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Warfare
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic understanding of  
the different dynasties that ruled throughout  
Chinese history.
Background
Military skills were very important in ancient China. 
Even scholars, who never usually fought, were 
expected to have these skills. Given the amount of 
civil fighting within China, these skills were often 
used. The armies were made up of peasants who 
were conscripted to fight for several years before they 
could return home. Some soldiers stayed in the army 
as regular soldiers after they had completed their 
conscripted time. Some found it exciting, while others 
enjoyed the money or the change in lifestyle.
Starter activity
In small groups, have students brainstorm around the 
topic of military forces. Why is it important to have an 
army? What skills should a good leader have? Discuss 
their answers as a class. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Students should read the Resource sheet, ‘Conflicts’, 
before completing the Activity sheet, ‘Fighting fit’. 
These work sheets provide some background on the 
conflicts that occurred in ancient China. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Weapons and gear’, provides 
students with a visual understanding of some of the 
weapons that were used in those times. Students 
identify weapons by matching illustrations with their 
descriptions. The Activity sheet, ‘Chariots’, presents 
a cloze activity introducing chariots and their role in 
warfare. 
The last Activity sheet, ‘The art of war’, looks at Sun 
Tzu’s ideas about war. This activity is intended to be 
done in pairs. Emphasise that there are no right or 
wrong answers, as different people will see different 
situations as ideal. This last activity is a great task to 
extend into a group discussion where students share 
their answers and the explanations for their decisions.
Extension ideas
• Have students research weapons that are used 
today. Students could create a poster comparing 
these modern weapons to ancient weapons.
• Students could research a famous warrior 
from ancient China, such as Sun Tzu. The 
following website may be of assistance: http://
scienceofstrategy.org/main/content/sun-tzus-life
• Show students the story of Hua Mulan – a fictional 
story about a woman who dressed as a man so she 
could fight in place of her father. Students could 
then write their own version. See 
http://www.yellowbridge.com/onlinelit/mulan.php
• Students could research other ancient Chinese 
weapons, then draw one and label it. See http://
history.cultural-china.com/en/182History5440.html
Objectives
• To learn about the gear and transport used by 
armies in ancient China
• To develop an understanding of the planning 
involved in preparing for battles
• To identify the importance of the army and 
military skills to ancient Chinese life

Achieve!   history – The ancient world: china 1
47
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Religion and beliefs
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.
Background
Religion was very important in ancient China, but 
many people did not consider themselves followers 
of one particular religion. Many Chinese followed 
Confucian ideas as well as Buddhism or Taoism. For 
many Chinese, the most important aspect of religion 
was the ancestor worship which, given the importance 
of family in ancient China, is not surprising. This 
ancestor worship may also be linked to the lowly 
status of women in ancient China. As a woman joined 
her husband’s family she left the worship of her 
ancestors to her father and brothers and was instead 
expected to support and protect her husband’s 
family and ancestors. This meant she was seen as 
less connected to her own ancestors, but not quite 
connected to her husband’s.
Starter activity
As a class, make a graph of students’ religions. This 
could include information such as religion, place of 
worship, frequency of attendance and importance 
of religion to their life. Hold a discussion about the 
similarities and differences in students’ religious 
beliefs and practices.
Resource and Activity sheets
Have students read the Resource sheet, ‘The four 
religions of China’, before they complete the Activity 
sheet, ‘Comparison of religions.’ Go through the 
results as a class. Students then work with a partner 
to create a rule that would be appropriate for each 
religion.
The Resource sheet, ‘Death and ancestor worship’, 
explores funeral customs and the practice of ancestor 
worship. In the Activity sheet, ‘Death’, students 
complete sentences and reorder sentences to 
consolidate their learning. 
The final Activity sheet, ‘Telling the future’, examines 
some of the methods astrologers and sages used to 
tell the future. Ensure that students understand the 
words in the word bank before starting this activity, 
although they should still be able to place them by 
context.
Extension ideas
• Students could research religion in modern China. 
What do most Chinese believe now?
• Each student could pick one of the religious leaders 
and research their life. There is plenty of information 
about Confucius and Buddha available, but very 
little is known about Lao Tzu.
• Students could write a short paragraph about the 
religion they follow, stating who the leader is, when 
the religion was started, beliefs, gods, who follows 
the religion and why.
Objectives
• To develop an understanding of the different 
religious beliefs present in ancient China
• To identify important practices in preparing for 
the afterlife and ancestor worship
• To compare and contrast burial practices of 
poor and rich people
• To explore methods of telling the future

Achieve!   history – The ancient world: china 1
53
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Trade
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of scale and 
distance in atlases and maps. They should also be 
familiar with the location of ancient China.
Background
Trade is always important in a developing civilisation. 
It exposes the people to different religions, views of 
the world and cultural experiences. In ancient China, 
trade was driven by one main product: silk. For a long 
time, nobody else was able to make silk. This gave the 
Chinese a monopoly on the product, making it both 
highly desirable and a symbol of wealth. 
Starter activity
Ask the students to look at some objects that they 
have with them in the classroom, such as their 
clothing, stationery, books, etc. In groups, have them 
find out where the items were made (look at their 
labels) and then, using an atlas or computer, map the 
distance the objects had to travel. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Silk’, introduces the development 
and importance of silk. The Resource sheet, ‘The Silk 
Road’, further explains the connection of silk to trade 
and why it was so important to the Chinese. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Maps and trading’, illustrates 
physical realities of trade, including the distances 
covered and the climates experienced. Check that 
students are comfortable interpreting scales in order 
to ensure that they understand the distances. It may 
also be helpful to use string to help the students 
measure, as the Silk Road was not straight and would 
be difficult to accurately measure using only a ruler.
The Resource sheet, ‘Contacts and conflicts’, outlines 
China’s interactions with other countries. Students 
then complete the map on the Activity sheet, ‘Trading 
with other countries’. They may need to refer back to 
the first Resource sheet, ‘The Silk Road’, as well as an 
atlas, when completing this activity. The answers to 
the final two questions on this sheet are likely to be: 
by sea – India, Japan and Korea. By road – Macedonia 
and Persia/Iran. Rome would probably have been a 
combination of the two. Looking at an atlas and the 
Silk Road map should make this fairly clear.
Extension ideas
• Have students imagine what life would be like if 
there was no trade, and they only had access to 
local products, then encourage them to write a 
diary entry depicting life under these conditions. 
Prompt them with questions such as: What can 
you eat? Can you still buy your favourite brand of 
clothes? Do you still have access to the same games 
and movies?
• Students could research how the Chinese made silk, 
and create a poster outlining the process. 
Objectives
• To develop an understanding of the 
importance of silk in ancient China
• To recognise the difficulties the Chinese faced 
in trading to other countries
• To identify the impacts of trading on ancient 
China

59
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Qin Shi Huang
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with the information 
about dynasties and timelines in Unit 1.
Background
Qin Shi Huang is an important character in ancient 
Chinese history, famous for his accomplishments. 
These include positives, such as the unification of 
China and the construction of the Great Wall of China, 
but also negatives, such as book burning and the loss 
of life that accompanied the construction of the Great 
Wall. He is perhaps best known now for his tomb, 
which was excavated in the 1970s. 
Starter activity
As a class, brainstorm the qualities that make a good 
leader. Which qualities are the most important? 
Discuss whether a leader in ancient times would have 
needed different characteristics to today’s leaders.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Qin Shi Huang’, introduces Qin 
Shi Huang and outlines how he united China. In the 
Activity sheet, ‘The man who united China,’ students 
complete sentences to consolidate their learning.
In the Activity sheet, ‘Burial and terracotta warriors’, 
students match difficult terms with their definitions. 
Some students may need to refer to a dictionary when 
completing this activity.
The Activity sheet, ‘Burning of the books’, presents a 
passage describing the book burning that happened 
during Qin Shi Huang’s reign. Students insert 
antonyms for some of the words used throughout  
the passage.
The final Activity sheet, ‘Great Wall of China’,  
introduces another of Qin Shi Huang’s major 
accomplishments, encouraging students to consider 
both the advantages and disadvantages of such a 
construction.
Extension ideas
• When Qin Shi Huang died he was buried with many 
possessions. This was because the Chinese believed 
that people would need these in the afterlife. 
Ask students to list ten things they could not live 
without, explaining why they are so important.
• Students could make a table highlighting Qin Shi 
Huang’s positive and negative characteristics. What 
made him a positive leader? What made him a 
negative leader? They could then conduct further 
research into his life and present this information in 
a poster or booklet. The following website may be 
of assistance: 
www.travelchinaguide.com/attraction/shaanxi/
xian/terra_cotta_army/qin_shihuang_1.htm
• Students could write a diary entry from the 
perspective of one of the Emperor’s wives, 
describing her feelings when he died.
• Students could research some of the possessions 
found in Qin Shi Huang’s tomb. See  
whc.unesco.org/en/list/441/andimperialtours.net/
blog/terracotta-warriors
Objectives
• To learn about the background of one the most 
famous Chinese emperors
• To develop an understanding of the impact 
that Qin Shi Huang had on China as we know  
it today
• To identify the beliefs and values that 
motivated many of Qin Shi Huang’s actions

Activity sheet – Introducing ancient China
Ancient China
When China was first settled, almost 4000 years ago, it was made up of many little kingdoms, 
each with its own ruler. This meant that for many years, nobody controlled all of China.
The kings who ruled the kingdoms often fought to become more powerful and to own 
more land. In the end, the most powerful king controlled the whole country and became 
known as the emperor of China. The Chinese believed that emperors were the ‘sons of 
heaven’, who had been chosen by the gods to rule. 
The position of emperor was usually handed down to the eldest son or nearest male relative. 
When China was ruled by the same family for a long period of time, this period was called a 
dynasty. Each dynasty was named after the family who ruled during that time. 
The ancient Chinese believed that their land was the centre of the universe. They called 
their country ‘The Middle Kingdom’.

Ruling families
The dynasties, or families, of ruling emperors were very powerful. They controlled the rest 
of the country and could tell people where to live or how to behave. If people disobeyed 
the emperor, they could be punished very severely.
The names of some dynasties can be spelt in many different ways in English. When 
Europeans first went to China they wanted to write down the Chinese names using the 
European alphabet. It was hard to get the sounds exactly right, so some names were spelt 
in different ways. For example, the Xia Dynasty is also referred to as the Hsia Dynasty.  
In Chinese there is only one way of writing and saying this name. 
Hint: Try saying Xia and Hsia out loud, or Zhou and Chou. Each pair sounds almost the same.
+ 
Circle the correct answer.
1  The ruling families of ancient China were called: (dynasties / movements / the mafia / 
the Simpsons).
2  The names of dynasties are often spelt in different ways because (elephants / 
Europeans / Americans / Australians) had trouble writing down some Chinese words 
using the European alphabet.
3 The emperors were the sort of people who:
• were very friendly to everyone.
• controlled the way people acted and would punish anyone who didn’t obey.
• had parties on Saturdays and invited everyone to come.
4 What would you like to know about ancient China? Write down at least three questions.

Recording time
Most religions base their calendar around important people or events in their religion.  
The Christian calendar is dated from the birth of Jesus. The term BC, or ‘Before Christ’, is 
used to refer to events that happened before his birth, and AD, or ‘Anno Domini’ (‘the year 
of our Lord’), refers to events that occurred after his birth. This makes it easier to work out 
when events happened in history.
Not everyone uses the Christian calendar. The year 2012 is the year 5772 for Jews and the 
year 1433 for Muslims. The term BCE, or ‘Before Common Era’, is sometimes used instead of 
‘Before Christ’, and CE, or ‘Common Era’, is sometimes used instead of ‘Anno Domini’.

Resource sheet – Geography of ancient China
Land and climate
China is the third largest country in the world. It is bordered by a sea on one side and a 
large mountain range on the other. These two features made it difficult for early Chinese 
people to travel and trade with the other important civilisations at the time, Rome and 
Greece. This meant that Chinese civilisation developed separately from other countries. 
The Chinese had to rely on themselves to create and make important objects because it 
was often too difficult to access ideas and inventions from other countries.
Deserts
In the north of China there is a large desert called the Gobi Desert. 
The Taklamakan Desert lies in the north-west of the country. The 
temperature in these deserts can range from 35 degrees Celsius to 
minus 35 degrees Celsius – from burning heat to freezing cold. 
Mountains
The Himalayas are a large mountain range in the south-west of 
China. In the lower parts of the mountains, the weather is tropical, 
but the tops of the mountains have alpine or snowy weather. 
Rainforests
The south-east of China is covered by tropical rainforest, bordered 
by the Pacific Ocean. The tropical areas often experience 
monsoon weather. A monsoon is a period of heavy rainfall that 
often leads to flooding.
