Growing food
Most civilisations began where people settled near 
water. Water is needed for so many things, such as 
drinking, cleaning and cooking. If a place has no easy 
access to water, people usually cannot live there.
The Yellow River (or Huang Ho) was one of the first 
places to be settled in China. It is named after the 
thick yellow earth surrounding it, called loess. When 
the Yellow River floods, the loess is washed over the 
land, where it helps crops to grow.
Although flooding is good for crops, it can damage buildings and people can drown. During 
the Shang Dynasty, the Chinese created irrigation channels to carry water to farms and 
stop the river flooding. There are only two main rivers in China (the Yellow River and the 
Yangtze), so man-made rivers called canals were also dug to transport water to other parts 
of the country. These canals became like highways for trade, enabling small boats to carry 
items from one place to another. They also meant people could catch fish to eat.
Access to water affects the type of food that can 
be grown in an area. 
• In both northern and southern China people 
grew leeks, garlic, carrots, cabbage  
and fruit. 
• In the south, because there was so much 
water, their main food was rice, which is 
grown in water-filled fields called paddies. 
• People in the north had less access to water, 
so they grew barley and wheat, which they 
used to make noodles and bread.

Resource sheet – Social structure
Social structure in ancient China
People in ancient China were organised into different social groups. A person’s position 
was usually based on their job. The highest-ranking member of the society was the 
emperor, because he was the most respected person. The lowest-ranking group were 
merchants. This was not because they were poor, but because their job was the least 
respected. In ancient China, respect and honour were very important. People who 
contributed the most to society were seen as the most honourable. This is why farmers, 
although they were quite poor, were still highly ranked in the social structure. 
There were servants and slaves in ancient China, but they were seen as so low that they 
were not thought of as part of society. Some servants could gain power, however, if they 
worked for the emperor and became his advisors. 
Emperor
The Emperor often had absolute power over his subjects. He was greatly 
respected and was seen as the ‘son of heaven’.
Government officials and warriors
Government officials were scholars who helped the emperor rule his 
kingdom. They worked on paperwork and were respected for their learning.
The warriors were from the ruling class. They were respected for their 
leadership abilities and military skills.
Farmers and peasants
Although farmers and peasants were often poor, they were respected 
for being landowners. They were often seen as the backbone of Chinese 
civilisation. It was believed that they made China strong.
Craftspeople
Craftspeople made beautiful and necessary objects. Although they made 
useful things, they were not respected because they did not own land. Their 
skills, however, kept them from being the lowest group in China.
Merchants and traders
Merchants and traders were often quite wealthy, but they were usually seen 
as untrustworthy. Because they did not make their own goods or own their 
own land they were the least respected group in society.

Resource sheet – Women
Women’s lives
In ancient China, men were usually the head of the family. They made all the decisions  
and worked to support the rest of the family. A man could even legally kill his children,  
if he wanted to. 
The birth of a female child was usually a disappointment. Her parents would often worry 
about how expensive her future wedding would be. Women could bring dishonour to 
their family by not behaving appropriately – people would believe that her parents had 
not taught her how a woman should behave. 
As they grew up, girls and women were often seen as only temporary members of their 
family. This is because when girls got married, they usually left their family to live with their 
husband’s family. The husband’s mother would then treat the new bride like a servant.
Many people, including scholars 
such as Confucius, believed that 
the home was the proper place for 
women. Women had to:
• keep away from guests
• spin silk or hemp into cloth
• sew
• weave
• cook
• care for the children
• be respectful
• yield to others’ wishes.
Some women were able to get jobs outside the house. They were usually from a scholar’s 
family and had some education. Some women worked as scholars themselves, and even 
wrote books, like Ban Zhao. Others became female physicians. This was allowed in order 
to protect the feelings of female patients, as male physicians were not permitted to touch 
or talk directly to women. Women could not become teachers or politicians, as they were 
not allowed to speak freely around men. This made it impossible for women to gain  
any real power. 
Women in ancient China were seen as inferior to men.

Historians do not know exactly when foot binding started. Some believe that it started during 
the Tang Dynasty (618–907 CE), but others have suggested the Sui, Han or Qin dynasties. The 
aim of foot binding was to make the feet less than seven centimetres long. Foot binding was 
usually done by mothers or aunts, who felt that they were giving their daughters or nieces 
a better life. This practice was usually done to girls in wealthier families, whose parents and 
future husbands could afford to look after a woman who could barely walk. Some peasant 
girls also had their feet bound, in the hope they would get a richer husband.

Activity sheet – Women
Ban Zhao 
Ban Zhao (approximately 45 CE–116 CE) was the most famous female historian in ancient 
China. She lived during the Han Dynasty. Her father, Ban Biao, was a scholar and her 
mother could also read and write. Ban Zhao was taught to do the same. She also had twin 
brothers; one became a scholar and the other became a general.
At the age of fourteen she was married to a local boy, Cao Shishu. In her husband’s house 
she was treated like a servant. Her life became even harder when her husband died 
young, leaving her alone with her children.
When her brother Ban Gu, the scholar, was executed, Ban Zhao returned home to finish 
the history book he had been writing. She finished writing The Book of Han, taught 
females in the royal family, became a librarian at court and wrote several books. While at 
court she also became a close advisor and lady-in-waiting to the Dowager Empress Deng, 
who was the regent for her infant son, the emperor.
Ban Zhao is best known for her book Lessons for Women. It is believed that this was written 
to instruct her daughters on how to behave in their husband’s house. Some historians see 
this book as telling women to follow men, while others believe that it is helping women.
+

Activity sheet – Everyday life
Medicine 
Ancient Chinese medicine was very different to today’s Western medicine. The ancient 
Chinese believed that the body was sacred and should not be damaged. This made 
it hard for them to learn about how the human body worked. Today, doctors conduct 
autopsies to examine the human body and learn more about it.
The Chinese mostly used herbs to fix health problems. They also used acupuncture, 
which involves putting lots of thin needles into pressure points in the body to help treat 
illnesses. People still use alternative forms of healing such as these. Sometimes sick people 
will use both Chinese and Western medicine. 
Chinese doctors became very good at diagnosing illnesses. They could sometimes 
work out what was wrong with someone by touching them and checking their pulse. 
Nowadays we use blood tests to find the problem.

Writing
Ancient Chinese language was first written over 3500 years ago. It is very different to 
modern Chinese. Chinese writing doesn’t use an alphabet like English does. We use the 
26 letters in our alphabet to make thousands of words. The Chinese use pictograms, or 
‘characters’, instead of letters. A pictogram is a picture used to represent a word. In English, 
‘China’ is written using five letters, but in Chinese it is shown with just one character. 
When the Chinese first developed their written language there were about 3000 
characters. Each character looked like the thing it represented. Over time, the shapes 
slowly changed so they were quicker to write. They ended up looking very different. 
The following table shows how some Chinese characters have changed over time.

(around 2000 CE)

By the Han Dynasty scholars were expected to learn about 8000 characters. Scholars and 
the wealthy were the only people in ancient China who were able to read and write.  
They were mostly men, although some wealthy girls or daughters of scholars were also 
taught to read and write.

Sport and recreation
The Chinese played many different sports, although the poorer people didn’t get much 
time to play because they were so busy working or farming. The Chinese enjoyed 
playing sports such as boxing, wrestling, polo, archery and shuttlecock. They also 
played a game called Touhu where they tried to throw arrows into a container. Sports 
were mostly played by men, although some women also took part.
+ 
1 Which sports are popular today? Which ones are your favourites?
 
 
 
 
 
 
Martial arts first began in China. This sport involves learning how to defend yourself 
without weapons. Many of the actions look like the movements of animals, which is 
not surprising, given the importance of farming in China.
2  Why might people in ancient China need to defend themselves without weapons? 
Who would have used these skills?
 
 
 
 
 
 
The ancient Chinese were very fond of music and created many musical instruments. 
They had one called a quin, which looked like a box with seven strings on it. They also 
played bamboo flutes and drums. Some people believe that the practice of foot binding 
began when dancers bound their feet to make their movements look light and graceful.

Resource sheet – Law and order
Honour and crimes
Honour was very important in ancient China. To have honour, the ancient Chinese had to 
earn the respect of the community and behave well as a member of their family. Families 
were the centre of ancient Chinese society. It was only by working together and following 
the head of the family that people were able to get things done. It was important to 
follow the laws in order to earn respect and have honour. People wanted to avoid 
breaking laws, which would bring shame to their family. 
Many ancient Chinese laws were about respecting the family ancestors and their burial 
grounds. There were rules about respecting parents and doing everything they asked.  
The people also had to protect their emperor. If the emperor was injured or killed,  
the whole country would be dishonoured. People who disobeyed the emperor were 
punished harshly.
Many ancient Chinese could not read. 
This made it difficult for them to know 
the law. Local officials and wealthy 
landowners in an area were supposed 
to tell their people about the laws and 
punishments. It was felt that if people 
knew the shame and loss of honour that 
would come from breaking a law, then 
they would obey.
Many ancient Chinese laws were designed to protect the emperor.

Resource sheet – Law and order
Punishments
The punishments for breaking laws in ancient China were very harsh. They were designed 
to make sure that people would obey the laws. Some crimes that we consider to be very 
minor were punished quite harshly. Fathers were even allowed to kill their own children if 
they misbehaved. 
These punishments may seem extreme, but families were essential to survival in ancient 
China. If one person on a farm failed to do their work, the whole family could starve. 
Obedience to family was highly important in ancient Chinese society. 
It was even a crime to tell officials that a family member had broken the law. Anyone who 
did this could be beaten 100 times. And if the information they gave was not true, the 
informant could be strangled.
Punishments in ancient China
• Beating with a bamboo stick was seen as a minor punishment.
• Students were beaten for misbehaving and to improve their learning.
• Pickpockets might be branded with red-hot metal on their arms.
• Other criminals could have their faces branded, be given into slavery or even  
be killed.
• A girl who insulted her parents might be strangled.
• One person who disagreed with the emperor was given two options: he could 
either commit suicide or become an eunuch.
• If someone committed a crime against the emperor they would be tortured and 
beheaded. A beheading was considered to be the most shameful punishment, 
because it meant that the noblest part of your body was removed.

Resource sheet – Warfare
Conflicts
China was involved in many early conflicts. Sometimes Chinese armies fought against the 
nomadic people of the deserts, the Xiongu. Because they were always moving from place 
to place, the nomads had excellent horse skills, which made them a feared enemy of the 
Chinese. The Chinese army also fought against bandits and robbers who tried to control 
wealthy areas, like trade routes. The Chinese believed that people who lived outside of 
China were barbarians, and they fought hard to prove that the Chinese were dominant.
Much of the time, however, the Chinese armies fought each other. In the early years of 
China, at the end of the Chou/Zhou period (1027–221 BCE), when the country was divided 
into many small kingdoms, the kings fought each other to take control of other kingdoms 
and make themselves more powerful. Whole cities were destroyed in these violent 
battles. Sometimes the leader of the losing side was killed as a human sacrifice. Troops 
who surrendered were often killed. Sometimes the fighting was so bad that the troops 
wore their armour day and night, until their bodies crawled with lice. 
One of the most powerful kings was Qin Shi Huang. Once he defeated all the other kings 
he became known as the ‘First Emperor’. From then on, the Chinese army worked to 
protect the emperor. This only became a problem when several different people claimed 
the throne. This happened often during the Three Kingdoms period (220–260 CE), as well 
as during the Dynasties of the North and South (317–589 CE).

Weapons and gear
In ancient China, the most respected weapon was the bow and arrow. Archery was used 
in the armies, but it was also used in other ways. Scholars shot arrows into targets to pick 
the questions they would answer in their exams. In some court cases, archery was used to 
help work out whether people were telling the truth. If they were able to hit the target, it

Soldiers used many weapons to protect themselves, such as spears for long-range 
fighting. Swords and sabres were also used, but because they were shorter, they were

Resource sheet – Religion and beliefs
The four religions of China
Folk religion
Folk religion is the oldest religion in China. It is so old that there is no identified 
founder of the religion. Its followers worshipped a number of different gods or spirits, 
including gods of nature, dragons and ancestors. They believed that if they prayed to 
the gods, they would be protected from misfortune. They also performed rituals to 
keep the gods happy. 
Buddhism
Buddhism was started in India in the 500s BCE by Prince Gautama, who later became 
known as Buddha, the enlightened one. Followers of Buddhism believe that following 
the middle path is the most important thing. This means not having too much or 
too little, as either would make you unhappy. The Chinese worshipped Buddha and 
Guanyin, the goddess of mercy. Buddhism appealed to many poor or mistreated 
Chinese, who felt that their lives were difficult.
Confucianism
Confucianism was started in China by a famous philosopher named Master Kong, 
whose name was later written as Confucius. He taught people about the importance 
of ancestor worship, tradition and family. One of his most important laws stated that 
people should be good to each other. Many followers were scholars, as Confucianism 
valued education. Although many Confucians believed that Heaven was their supreme 
being, they cared more about behaving the right way than about gods. 
Daoist/Taoist
The Daoist or Taoist religion was about freedom from rules. This religion was created in 
China around the 300s BCE, possibly by a man named Lao Tzu. Instead of good or bad, 
Daoists believed in the balance of yin and yang, or light and dark. They believed that 
each person had 36 000 deities, or god-like figures, inside them.

Resource sheet – Religion and beliefs
Death and ancestor worship
Ancestor worship
Many of the people in ancient China practised ancestor worship. They believed that their 
deceased ancestors, such as grandparents and great-grandparents, were looking after 
them. In return for this protection, the living family members had to practise special 
rituals to protect and worship their ancestors. 
Death
The Chinese would bury their loved ones with items that they had needed in life. If they 
were rich this might include clothes, food, jewels and even animals. An extremely rich 
person might even get a jade suit made for their funeral. If the person was poor, though, 
they would be buried with clothes and food that were made out of paper. Some rich 
people were buried with animals and slaves to serve them in their next life. Sometimes the 
slaves and animals were killed and buried. Other times, however, they were buried alive.
Funerals
Family and friends would dress in white and gather at a funeral to grieve together. Rich 
people would pay for enormous tombs in mountainsides and hire musicians to entertain. 
The poor could only make little straw huts to show their respect for their relatives. 
Children were expected to mourn their parents for three years. During that time they 
would wear only white, and would also complete special rituals for their parents.
Emperors and extremely wealthy people would sometimes be buried in a jade suit.

Silk
Nobody knows exactly how silk was discovered. One story suggests it was discovered 
around 2600 BCE, when Empress Leizu was playing in the garden near some mulberry 
bushes. Some small caterpillars were eating the mulberry leaves, and a cocoon dropped 
into a bowl of hot water. A fine silk thread unwound from the cocoon. The empress was so 
fascinated by it that she learned to weave the strands together to make silk. 
At first, silk was only for the emperor and his most prized subjects. Because it was 
connected to royalty, silk became very popular. Huge fields of mulberry trees were  
planted so more silk could be produced. The silk threads were harvested and then woven 
into beautiful, silky material. The Chinese also invented looms to make their silk finer  
and more luxuriant.
As silk became more popular, it was produced on an enormous scale. By around 110 BCE, 
the Chinese government had 5 million rolls of silk in reserve. The emperors had so much 
silk that they sometimes used it to pay their soldiers. The Emperor Wu Ti (140 BCE–87 BCE) 
handed out more than a million pieces of silk to the soldiers who worked on the Great 
Wall of China.

Resource sheet – Trade
The Silk Road
Silk was one of the most important discoveries in ancient China. It led to the development 
of trade with other countries, who desperately wanted some silk to show how rich and 
powerful they were. The Romans and Greeks called China ‘the land of silk’.
Many Chinese merchants travelled west on camels. Camels were slow – they could only 
travel about five kilometres an hour – but they could carry about 180 kilograms of supplies 
and go for 17 days without water. The merchants travelled through difficult environments 
and conditions, including deserts, sandstorms and cold, dangerous mountain trails, where 
they were constantly under threat from bandits. 
Because so many merchants were travelling along this road to sell silk, it became known 
as the Silk Road. The Chinese merchants traded silk for horses, foreign foods, jewels and 
rare animals and birds. During the Han Dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE) silk was so popular that a 
special government office was set up to control sales. 
Because the merchants had to travel so far, silk was extremely expensive. Some 
westerners tried to get silkworms so they could make silk themselves, but the Chinese 
merchants were forbidden to reveal the secret of making silk. Anyone who told foreigners 
how to make silk would be tortured to death.
The Silk Road connected China to the countries in the west.

Resource sheet – Trade
Contacts and conflicts
China was often a very isolated country. It was surrounded on all sides by mountains, 
deserts and treacherous seas, which made it very difficult to travel in or out.
Despite this, an increase in trade led to quite a lot of contact between China and other 
countries, particularly Italy, where silk became an expensive but familiar item. The Chinese 
called Rome ‘the other China’ because of the similarities between them. 
It was mostly merchants who travelled to and from China, including merchants from 
India, Persia, Japan and Korea who bought and sold Chinese products. However, many 
countries also sent envoys. Envoys were not trying to sell a product. Instead, they were 
trying to learn about the other country and develop a relationship with them. Eventually, 
so many foreigners travelled to China that they had to make laws stating whether 
foreigners could own land or marry Chinese women.
Sometimes the Chinese used trade and gifts to protect their country. A nomadic people 
called the Xiongu destroyed many areas of China. They invaded cities and towns, where 
they stole possessions and slaves, killed people and destroyed houses. The Chinese 
decided to give the Xiongu gifts such as farm tools and seeds, as well as silk, to make 
peace with them. Eventually the Xiongu stopped fighting the Chinese because they did 
not want to lose these gifts.

Resource sheet – Qin Shi Huang
Qin Shi Huang
Qin Shi Huang (259 BCE–210 BCE) is one of the most famous emperors in Chinese history. 
Although there were many emperors before him, Qin Shi Huang is often considered the 
first emperor of China. This is because he was the first to unite most of the country. The 
emperors before him ruled a much smaller area.
Qin Shi Huang was born around 259 BCE. He was called Prince Cheng at that time, and 
his father ruled the small kingdom of Qin/Ch’in. The Chou/Zhou Dynasty had gradually 
disintegrated into small kingdoms and states, and the rulers of these small kingdoms 
fought to take over neighbouring kingdoms. Prince Cheng was fourteen when he became 
the King of Qin. He spent the next twenty-five years fighting and taking control of all the 
other states. In the end he gained so much land and power that the remaining kingdoms 
surrendered to him.
Once King Cheng gained control of all the other states he changed his name to Shi Huang, 
which means ‘first emperor’. ‘Qin’ refers to the name of his state. He was so powerful that 
the name of his small kingdom, Qin/
Ch’in, became the name of the entire 
land – China. By calling himself Qin Shi 
Huang, he was calling himself the first 
emperor of all China. Shi Huang was 
convinced that his dynasty, the Qin 
Dynasty, was so powerful that it would 
last for ten thousand years.  
It lasted only fifteen.

Qin Shi Huang was very superstitious, and believed that potions and spells could be used  
to protect him. He was terrified of death – when he talked about his dynasty ruling for  
ten thousand years, he wanted to rule for that entire time. He often sought out elixirs that 
would help him live forever. 
Although Qin Shi Huang hoped to live forever, he also planned for his death. As soon as he 
became emperor he arranged for work to begin on his burial tomb. It was enormous. There 
was room for 7000 terracotta warriors, 600 clay horses and 100 chariots, swords, bows, arrows 
and axes. His tomb was the size of about 50 football fields. He was not buried alone, either. All 
his wives who did not have sons were buried with him, alongside the workers who knew the 
secrets of his tomb.
There were 700 000 workers who helped build the tomb. They also put precious stones in the 
ceiling, and made the objects that were in his tomb. They believed that he would need all his 
possessions and wives in the afterlife.

1 
Rules can come under more than one classification. ‘Do not lie’, for example, can be seen 
as a social rule as well as a legal rule. Identify three social ramifications of lying. 
 
 
 
2

of breaking the rule.
 
 
 
 
REMEMBER 
Three common types of rules are legal rules (laws), membership rules and social rules. 
Breaking a rule usually has consequences.
Case study: Breaking the rules
Al was not in the mood to go to school today. He’d been having a lot of trouble with some of the 
smaller kids lately. They used to fear him and scatter as he approached. Then, when his attempt at 
facial piercing went horribly wrong, the little kids stopped running and started giggling. 
Al stomped angrily along the footpath. A group of women walked towards him and stared 
at his wound. Al picked his nose right in their faces, making the gash look twice the size. 
He hoped they would say something, but they just looked repulsed and hurried away. 
At lunchtime, a Year 7 boy pointed and laughed at Al as he walked by. Al grabbed the kid 
by the collar, lifted him into the air and threatened to cut him. The boy wriggled madly, 
then started to howl and cry. Al smiled, satisfied, but then a teacher came over and made 
him let the kid go. 
The principal wanted to search Al’s bag. Al refused, even though he suspected he would

1

REMEMBER 
The head of government is the leader of the political party in power. Australia’s head of 
state has mainly ceremonial duties and represents the country internationally.
Case study: November 1975
Just how powerful is the head of state? For most of the 20th century it was assumed the 
governor-general had no real power. Little more than a figurehead, the governor-general’s 
duties were traditionally seen as ceremonial. These duties include approving legislation, 
appointing ministers and dissolving the lower house of parliament at election time. By 
convention, the governor-general always acted on the advice of the prime minister.
Even so, the governor-general possesses certain powers that can be exercised without 
the advice of the government. Known as reserve powers, the Queen’s representative has 
the ability to appoint and dismiss a prime minister. Such a tremendous capacity can only 
be exercised in very limited circumstances, for example, if the prime minister loses the 
support of parliament in a ‘no confidence’ vote and then fails to resign.
In November 1975, the Governor-General Sir John Kerr made history by using his reserve 
powers to dismiss Gough Whitlam’s Labor government. The Whitlam government was 
facing a financial crisis. Although the Labor government had a majority in the lower house, 
the Liberal Party had a majority in the upper house. The Liberal Party deferred Supply Bills 
in the upper house, meaning they prevented the government from getting the money it 
needed to run the country. Sir John Kerr broke the deadlock by dismissing Whitlam from 
office. Malcolm Fraser, the leader of the opposition, was appointed caretaker (temporary) 
prime minister and an election was called. The Liberal Party won the election. The Supply 
Bills were passed.

REMEMBER 
Lawmaking powers held only by the Commonwealth are called exclusive powers, 
those held only by the states are called residual powers and shared powers are called 
concurrent powers.
Case study: Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983) 158 CLR 1
At first glance, it appears the states have strong legislative powers. However, there are ways in 
which federal laws can override these powers. One way comes straight from the Constitution. 
Section 109 states if there is a clash between a federal and state law, the Commonwealth law 
will prevail and the inconsistent part of the state law will be invalid. 
There are also situations where the Commonwealth may intrude on a state’s residual 
powers and stop the state laws operating. This was shown in the Tasmanian Dams Case. 
The Tasmanian government wanted to increase the state’s capacity to create electricity. It 
passed a law allowing the construction of a hydroelectric dam on the Gordon River, which 
would have flooded part of the Franklin River, an area of great natural beauty. Australia 
has duties under an international agreement to protect areas that are designated World 
Heritage Sites. Responding to public outcry, the Commonwealth passed a law preventing 
construction of the dam.
The Tasmanian government objected, and the case was heard by the High Court. 
The Commonwealth claimed it could override state laws to comply with Australia’s 
international obligations. It claimed it was given this power over external affairs by the 
Constitution. A majority of the High Court agreed and the dam was not built.

REMEMBER 
In Australia, the separation of powers includes:
• legislative or lawmaking power (given to parliaments)
• executive or administrative power (given to the Queen and her representatives – the 
governor-general and state governors; in practice, wielded by government ministers 
and departments)
• judicial power (given to courts and tribunals).

Case study: The power to remove judges
The independence of the judiciary is the most important aspect of the separation 
of powers. Judges cannot be members of either the executive or legislative arms of 
government. Neither can they be controlled or directed by these arms.
But the executive chooses and appoints judges. Governments might select judges that 
have similar values and opinions as their own members. Indeed, several judges were 
once members of parliament. Governments come and go, however, and the judges may 
continue to preside throughout many changes of government.
A greater danger would exist if the executive had the power to dismiss judges if they 
disagreed with their judgements. Is this actually the case? Section 72 of the Australian 
Constitution gives the executive the power to remove judges for ‘proved misbehaviour or 
incapacity’. This nearly happened to a High Court judge.
Justice Lionel Murphy was a radical and outspoken judge who was responsible for many 
reforms. He had once been a member of parliament and he served as attorney-general for 
the federal Labor government in the 1970s.

In the mid-1980s, Murphy was accused of attempting to pervert the course of justice –  
more specifically, to influence a court case in favour of someone he called his ‘little mate’. 
He was eventually found not guilty, and he praised the jury system. His radical judgements, 
however, had upset the conservative factions of the government. Moves were made to 
remove Murphy for misbehaviour by passing a law through parliament.
Sadly Murphy was diagnosed with incurable cancer. The action was dropped. The ability 
of the Commonwealth Parliament to remove a High Court judge has not been finally 
determined.

Case study: Forming a minority government
Usually there is a clear winner following an election. But in the 2010 federal election, 
neither of the major parties secured enough seats in parliament to govern in their  
own right. 
The House of Representatives is composed of 150 members. For a party to gain an 
outright majority they need to win at least 76 seats. This did not happen. The result is 
known as a hung parliament. A hung parliament means no party can pass laws without 
the support of other parties and/or the independents.

7 Parliament
This is not unprecedented in Australia. Hung state parliaments occur occasionally, but the 
only other time there was a hung federal parliament was in 1940, after the outbreak of 
World War II. 
The seats won in the 2010 federal election were: Labor Party 72, Liberal Party 44, Liberal 
National Party of Queensland 21, National Party 7, Independents 4, Country Liberal Party 1, 
Greens Party 1.
Both Labor and the Coalition (the Liberal Party, Liberal National Party of Queensland 
and the National Party) tried to gain the support of others in order to create a minority 
government. In the meantime, Julia Gillard, who was prime minister prior to the election, 
continued as caretaker prime minister until the issue could be resolved. If the issue had 
been unable to be resolved, another election may have been held. That was unnecessary, 
however, and Gillard’s Labor Party was able to form a minority government.

Case study: Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC562
The law of negligence is the classic example of common law evolving where no statutory 
law existed. In the past it was not possible for the victim of another person’s carelessness 
to sue if there was no contract between them. Gradually, however, courts started finding 
liability. 
In Donoghue v Stevenson, an unfortunate woman drank a bottle of ginger beer, only to 
find the remains of a decomposed snail in the bottle. She suffered gastroenteritis and 
severe shock. She had no contract with the ginger beer manufacturer, but the court was 
prepared to say the manufacturer owed her a duty of care. This was the start of a whole 
new area of law, and there is now comprehensive legislation that deals with negligence.
REMEMBER 
Judges can make laws, as well as interpret and apply laws. Court-made law is called 
common law. Judges traditionally interpret statutes according to the literal rule, 
mischief rule, golden rule and other language rules.

REMEMBER 
Customary laws are social rules given the status of law due to long usage. Although 
unwritten, customary law is traditionally considered binding by Aboriginal Australians. 
Case study: Customary law
Bill lived in a remote Aboriginal community. One night, Bill and his friend Jack had a few 
drinks together. A disagreement sprang up concerning Bill’s ex-girlfriend, now Jack’s wife. 
The men started to fight. The situation escalated and Bill broke Jack’s nose.
The tribal elders applied their customary laws and decided the appropriate punishment 
was retribution. Jack was instructed to spear Bill in the thigh. Jack was nervous and 
misjudged his aim. He hit an artery, causing severe bleeding. Bill nearly bled to death but 
recovered after receiving emergency medical treatment. 
Jack did not intend to cause such a serious injury. He was arrested by the police and 
charged with attempted murder.
2

ruling? Explain your answer. 
 
 
3

his customary laws?

International law develops through international treaties, conventions and other types 
of agreements. A country can become a signatory to a treaty or convention, but an 
international law only operates in that country if the country ratifies the agreement and 
passes legislation to implement it.
Case study: Northern Territory Emergency Response (NTER)
Australia ratified the International Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Racial 
Discrimination and then passed the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth).
When a nation ratifies the convention, it agrees to various undertakings, including:
• not to engage in actions of racial discrimination
• not to sponsor or support racial discrimination by any person or body
• to review government policies that are discriminatory and to amend the law
• to prohibit racial discrimination, hatred and violence
• to ensure remedies for victims of racial discrimination
• to combat prejudices through education.
Has Australia fulfilled its obligations? A report on child abuse in Indigenous Australian 
communities in 2007 led to an intervention by the Howard government. Called the 
Northern Territory Emergency Response (NTER), the action sparked indignation throughout 
the international community. 
The goals of the NTER were to protect women and children by increasing the presence 
of police in the relevant communities and restricting alcohol. Welfare quarantining was

11 Law reform
The following newspaper article is fictional. While reading it, keep in mind that the ability to 
legislate regarding law and order is a residual state power.
REMEMBER 
Laws need to change and develop to keep up with society’s changing attitudes. Calls  
for change can come from political parties, pressure groups or other organisations,  
and judges.
Teenage curfew causes chaos
27 February 2017, Australia 
GKG Press
Mass demonstrations and riots have broken out in response to a proposed curfew. 
Teenagers across the country have taken to the streets in a show of unity, waving placards 
and shouting slogans.
The spark that ignited the flame is a proposed law by the new federal government, 
which plans to impose an 11pm curfew on everyone under the age of 20. If passed, any 
teenagers found in public after 11pm will be arrested and held in overnight cells. Parents 
will be charged a $500 ‘holding fee’ per night of incarceration.
‘This is the only way to stop teenage drinking and violence’, said Siobhan State, the 
Minister of the newly created Commonwealth Department of Criminal Prevention. 
‘Children have been given too much freedom in the past, and they have all turned into 
drug-taking, body-piercing, handbag-snatching, tattooed criminals.’
Violence has erupted in most major cities as students express their disbelief and fury, but 
in each case protest has been met with strong-arm tactics by the law. Many young people 
have been hospitalised. Some commentators suggest it is only a matter of time before 
there is a fatality.
‘This is unacceptable’, said Jon Smyth, professor of law. ‘It is an abrogation of young 
people’s fundamental rights and a denial of human liberty. My colleagues and I are 
taking immediate action by writing a paper questioning the constitutional validity of the 
proposed law. A complaint to the United Nations Human Rights Committee is also being 
considered.’
‘That’s exactly the attitude I’d expect’, responded Ms State. ‘I blame the parents and 
the educational institutions for putting such ideas into young people’s heads. It’s time 
someone takes a stand for law and order, and this new government will not shy away 
from that responsibility.’

1 
Explain why is it so important that justice is seen to be done. 
 
 
 
 
 
REMEMBER 
Justice is hard to define, but a just law or judgement should have the characteristics of 
equality, fairness and access. Openness is essential for carrying out justice.
Case study: Equality of treatment
Four people are caught speeding along the same busy road at the same time. They are 
travelling through a school zone, with a 40 km/h speed limit. The limit when the school 
zone is not in operation is 70 km/h. Each driver is clocked travelling at 69 km/h while 
the school zone is in operation and each is fined the same sum.
Rachel, 28, is a single mother. She has never been booked before. She is picking up her 
six-year-old son from school but is running late because a work meeting ran over time.  
She is frantic because her ex-husband made a few attempts in the past to pick up their 
child without authority. Rachel is worried her ex might try to abduct their son if she is  
not there in time. 
Jason, 44, has been booked for speeding on several occasions, and has had his licence 
suspended more than once. He is a busy executive whose motto is ‘Time is money’. He 
often risks speeding fines, seeing them merely as a cost of business. For him, it is cheaper 
to pay the occasional fine than to lose money by spending more time on the road.
Ellie, 17, just received her provisional licence. It is the first time she is driving alone. 
She is excited but also nervous. Her mobile phone starts to ring but she ignores it. The 
distraction was enough, however, for her to not notice the school zone sign. Ellie is a high 
school student living with her parents. She has no income of her own.
Alfred, 79, has been driving for more than 60 years and has a perfect record. He has just 
learnt his wife is suffering from terminal cancer and has a few months left to live. He 
cannot concentrate on anything else. Alfred is on the age pension and is unsure if he can 
afford to give his wife a decent funeral.

Does equality of treatment lead to equal outcomes? Consider the fictional case study on the

offence – and for creating the same risk to the community? Explain your reasoning. 
 
 
 
3

experience. Do you think these should be taken into account? If so, who should receive  
the harshest penalty? 
 
 
 
4 
Another issue that distinguishes the offenders is financial position. A $200 fine would 
be much harder for Alfred to bear than Jason, for instance. Do you think their financial 
circumstances should be taken into account? Why or why not? 
 
 
 
5

it make no difference to the penalty? How would your answer differ if one of the drivers was 
intoxicated? 
 
 
 
 
6 
Nobody was hurt in the scenario. Assume now that a young child was knocked down and 
critically injured by one of the speeding drivers. Would your answers to the above questions 
stay the same? If not, how would they change?

Case study: Human rights in the Constitution
High Court judges are sometimes prepared to find that human rights are implied in the 
Australian Constitution. An example is the landmark case of Australian Capital Television v 
Commonwealth (1992) 177 CLR 106.
The case arose due to a challenge to the Political Broadcasts and Political Disclosures Act 
1991 (Cth). The Act banned the broadcast of political material leading up to an election.  
A majority of the High Court held that the Act infringed an implied right in the 
Constitution. Sections 7 and 24 of the Constitution provide for the election of 
senators and members of the House of Representatives. This, as well as the system 
of representative government created by the Constitution, was held to mean that 
Australians should be able to freely discuss political matters. In other words, there is 
an implied freedom of political discussion and communication in Australia. The Act in 
question infringed this right, and so the ban was declared to be invalid. 
Later High Court cases widened and extended the scope of this implied right. However, 
more recent High Court cases restricted it again. The implied right still exists, but its 
scope keeps changing.

Case study: Discrimination in the workplace
Ms Evans was an intelligence analyst with the National Crime Authority. She was a single 
mother and had to take a considerable amount of carer’s leave to look after her sick child. 
She was reprimanded even though she did not exceed her entitlements. Allegedly her 
manager said, ‘You hold a key position and someone like you has to be there 100 per cent’ 
and ‘If I had known of your situation I would never have hired you’. Evans was put under 
pressure to not take carer’s leave, was moved to a different team, and her contract was 
not renewed.
Section 14(2) of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) states that:
It is unlawful for an employer to discriminate against an employee on the ground of 
the employee’s sex, marital status, pregnancy or potential pregnancy: 
(a) in the terms or conditions of employment that the employer affords the 
employee; 
(b) by denying the employee access, or limiting the employee’s access, to 
opportunities for promotion, transfer or training, or to any other benefits associated 
with employment; 
(c) by dismissing the employee; or 
(d) by subjecting the employee to any other detriment.
The case went before the Federal Magistrates Court, where the magistrate agreed 
the employer breached the Act: Evans v National Crime Authority [2003] FMCA 375. He 
found that Evans was dismissed and discriminated against on the grounds of parental 
responsibility.

Case study: Equity and the law
The British adversarial system saw the development of the common law courts. 
Historically, these courts required a rigid adherence to the rules of evidence and 
procedure. This often led to injustices and harsh decisions. Medieval litigants (people 
involved in lawsuits) were able to petition the king to ‘do equity’ for them – that is, to 
ensure fairness and justice. Equity eventually evolved into a body of law that ran parallel 
to the common law and relieved some of its harshness. For example, it protects weak 
parties when they are taken advantage of by stronger parties.
The High Court case Blomley v Ryan (1956) 99 CLR 362 involved the sale of a farm 
for a very low price by an intoxicated elderly man. The buyer knew of the old man’s 
drinking spree and even brought a bottle of rum to the negotiations. The High Court 
held that because the buyer took advantage of the seller’s condition, equity would not 
allow specific performance. In other words, the party taking advantage of the weaker 
party cannot insist the contract be performed. The court described other factors and 
vulnerabilities that could lead to a similar result, including poverty, illness and illiteracy.

REMEMBER 
Trial by jury is one of the most important safeguards in the Australian legal system. Jury 
members are chosen at random, representing the impartiality and common sense of 
society. Some courts and states require unanimous verdicts; others require majority 
verdicts. A unanimous verdict is one that every member of a jury agrees on. A majority 
verdict is one that a majority – but not all – of a jury agrees on.

Raymond was charged with aggravated assault causing harm. His case was heard by a judge and 
jury. The jury returned a verdict of guilty. The jury then proceeded to sentence Raymond to six 
years’ imprisonment.

overwhelming. It cannot possibly be interpreted in the manner suggested by the defendant.  
I hereby direct you to return a verdict of guilty.’

4

5

6

b Is the High Court itself bound to follow its own previous rulings? 
 
 
7 
Putting aside legal matters for the moment, purely on a matter of policy, do you agree with 
Hinch’s position or do you think sex offenders’ names should be suppressed? Outline both 
sides of the argument and then reach your own conclusion. 
 
 
 
 
8 
Courts should only consider legal matters, and not matters of government policy. Discuss. 
 
 
Case study: Appealing to the High Court
Controversial Melbourne radio host Derryn Hinch launched a ‘Name Them and Shame 
Them’ campaign regarding sex offenders. He handed a petition to the Victorian premier 
during a rally at Parliament House. The petition demanded that parliament change laws 
so that judges and magistrates cannot suppress the names of serious sex offenders, 
unless such identification also identifies a victim. 
During the course of the rally, Hinch publicly named two repeat offenders. This and a 
publication on his website led to him being charged with breaching section 42 of the 
Serious Sex Offenders Monitoring Act 2005 (Vic). He was convicted by the Magistrates 
Court and appealed to the Supreme Court. The appeal failed, but he was granted the  
right to appeal to the High Court.
In Hogan v Hinch (2011) HCA 4, Hinch’s lawyer argued that section 42 was invalid under the 
Australian Constitution, which implied that all court proceedings be carried out in public. Counsel 
also claimed the section infringed the implied constitutional freedom of political communication. 
The High Court analysed the arguments and considered previous case law. Hinch’s arguments 
were held not to be supported, and so the appeal failed. He was sent back to the Magistrates 
Court for sentencing and received five months’ home detention.

REMEMBER 
Alternative dispute resolution (ADR) methods include complaining to relevant bodies, 
mediation and arbitration. In mediation, parties reach their own solution with the help 
of a mediator. In arbitration, the arbitrator makes a ruling that can be imposed.
Case studies: ADR and self-help
Katy bought a hairdryer from a department store. It cost $195. Katy used it daily for two 
months and had no problems. After that time, the hairdryer started to get very hot 
when she used it and Katy could smell her hair burning, even on the lowest setting. She 
was worried it would ruin her hair, so she stopped using it. She wants to take it back to 
the store and get a replacement. She remembers being told it had a one-year warranty. 
However, she no longer has the receipt or even the box that it came in. Katy paid with 
cash, so she has no credit card record of the purchase. Sadly Katy did not pick Legal 
studies as an elective, so she has no idea what to do. She turns to you, her good friend, 
for advice.

Katy attempt each approach? Why or why not?

Roy suspected a prowler was targeting his house. On several occasions, his teenage

adrenaline, Roy was rougher than he needed to be and ended up breaking the prowler’s

sued for assault.

Commercial whaling 
Commercial whaling – the harvesting of whales, mostly for meat – is carried out by a number of countries. 
Australia is one of many nations opposed to commercial whaling. Commercial whaling is regulated by the 
International Whaling Commission (IWC). The IWC is responsible for protecting whales around the world. 
Whaling has been practised for centuries in some parts of the world. It is considered an integral part of 
some traditional cultures in places such as Greenland and Alaska. Today, whaling is a highly controversial 
practice. Many countries are against it on environmental grounds – a number of whale species are 
threatened and their populations continue to decline. 
Conservation groups and other non-government organisations protest at many levels about commercial 
whaling – from political lobbying to physically preventing whaling activities at sea.
As the number of whales has decreased over the years, the whaling industry has changed to new locations, 
new target species and new harvesting techniques.
The move by many nations to protect the whales in their waters is relatively recent. The benefits of 
protection are both environmental and economic – many argue that whale-watching tourism is more 
profitable than commercial whaling. Even though the IWC exists to regulate whaling and protect whales, it 
is limited as a governing body. Nations do not have to belong to it, and therefore are not bound by its 
rulings on the industry – such as the introduction of quotas.
Commercial whaling – research
